phy_ocra.4.0.summary: A force is a push or a pull that arises when **two objects interact**. Objects can interact **by contact** (normal contact force, friction, air resistance, tension) or **at a distance through a field** (gravity, electrostatic and magnetic forces). Every interaction involves a **pair of objects** and produces a force **on each object**: the two forces are equal in size, opposite in direction and of the same type, and they act on different objects. Forces are **vectors**, so we show them as arrows with a size and a direction.

core.p: A force is a push or pull on an object caused by its interaction with another object. Forces can change an object's speed, direction of motion or shape.
bullets: Force is measured in **newtons (N)**.
Force is a **vector**: it has **magnitude (size) and direction**.
Forces are drawn as **arrows**: the length shows the size, the arrowhead shows the direction.
A force always needs **two objects** - one exerting and one receiving it.
Forces can be measured with a **newtonmeter (force meter)**, which uses a spring.

callouts.p: A **force** is a push or a pull that acts on an object due to its **interaction with another object**.

core.p: **Contact forces** act only when the objects are physically touching. They come from the electrical forces between particles on the two surfaces when they are squeezed or rubbed together.
bullets: **Normal contact force (reaction force)**: a surface pushes back on an object pressing on it, at **90 degrees to the surface**.
**Friction**: opposes the sliding (or attempted sliding) of two surfaces over each other; acts **parallel to the surface**.
**Air resistance (drag)**: friction from air on a moving object; opposes motion and **increases with speed**.
**Water resistance (drag)**: the same idea in a liquid.
**Tension**: the pull in a stretched rope, string or cable.
**Upthrust**: the upward push of a fluid on an object in it.

head: Contact force
Direction
Example
rows: At 90 degrees to the surface, away from it
Table pushing up on a book

callouts.p: In physics **normal** means **at right angles (90 degrees) to the surface** - that is why it is called the normal contact force.

core.p: **Non-contact forces** act between objects that are **not touching**. Each object is surrounded by a **field**, and another object placed in that field feels a force.
bullets: **Gravitational force (weight)**: attraction between any two **masses**; always attractive.
**Electrostatic force**: between **charged** objects; like charges **repel**, unlike charges **attract**.
**Magnetic force**: between **magnets** or magnetic materials; like poles repel, unlike poles attract.
Non-contact forces get **weaker as the distance between the objects increases**.
Gravity is very weak unless one object has a huge mass, such as the Earth.
**Weight = mass x gravitational field strength** (W = mg), g = 9.8 N/kg on Earth.

callouts.p: A **non-contact force** acts between objects that are **not touching**, through a **field** (gravitational, electric or magnetic).

core.p: OCR expects you to recall the ways objects interact: by **gravity**, **electrostatics**, **magnetism** and **contact**. Every force you meet at GCSE fits one of these.
bullets: **Gravity**: masses attract (Earth and Moon, you and the Earth).
**Electrostatics**: charges attract or repel (a rubbed balloon and hair).
**Magnetism**: magnetic poles attract or repel (fridge magnet and fridge door).
**Contact**: surfaces push or rub (normal contact force and friction).
Contact forces are really electrostatic forces between the particles of touching surfaces, which is why they need very small distances.

callouts.p: When asked how two objects interact, name the type (gravitational, electrostatic, magnetic or contact) and the two objects involved.

core.p: Forces always come in **pairs**. When object A exerts a force on object B, object B exerts a force on object A at the same time. These two forces form an **interaction pair**.
bullets: The two forces are **equal in size**.
They act in **opposite directions**.
They act on **different objects** (one on A, one on B).
They are the **same type of force** (both gravitational, both contact, etc.).
They act **at the same time** - neither comes first.
Example: the Earth pulls you down with your weight; **you pull the Earth up** with an equal gravitational force.
Because they act on different objects, the two forces in a pair **never cancel each other out**.

callouts.p: An interaction pair is **two forces of the same type**, **equal in size**, **opposite in direction**, acting on **two different objects**.

core.p: Contact interactions also give pairs. A book resting on a table pushes down on the table, and the table pushes up on the book.
bullets: Book pushes **down on the table** (contact force); table pushes **up on the book** (normal contact force).
These two contact forces are an interaction pair: equal, opposite, on different objects.
Your foot pushes **backwards on the ground**; friction from the ground pushes you **forwards**. This is how you walk.
A swimmer pushes water **backwards**; the water pushes the swimmer **forwards**.
A rocket pushes exhaust gases **down**; the gases push the rocket **up**.

core.p: Students often confuse an interaction pair with two balanced forces on one object. Both involve equal and opposite forces, but balanced forces act on the **same object**.
bullets: Book's **weight** (Earth pulls book down) and **normal contact force** (table pushes book up) both act on the **book**, so they are **balanced forces**, not an interaction pair.
They are also **different types** (gravitational and contact).
The partner of the book's weight is the **book pulling the Earth upwards**.
The partner of the table's push on the book is the **book pushing down on the table**.
Test: same type? different objects? If both yes, it is an interaction pair.

callouts.p: Weight and the normal contact force on a resting book are **not** an interaction pair - they act on the same object and are different types of force.

core.h: Why both objects do not move equally
core.p: If the forces in a pair are equal, why does the apple move towards the Earth but the Earth hardly moves? Because the effect of a force depends on the mass it acts on.
bullets: The same size force gives a **small mass a large acceleration** and a **large mass a tiny acceleration**.
The Earth's mass is so enormous that its acceleration towards the apple is far too small to notice.
When two skaters push off each other, the lighter skater moves away faster.
Equal forces do **not** mean equal effects.

core.p: Because forces have size and direction, they are vectors and we draw them as arrows. This lets you compare and combine them.
bullets: Draw arrows **from the object** in the direction the force acts.
Make the **arrow length proportional to the size** of the force.
Label each arrow with its **name and size** (e.g. weight 20 N).
Scalars (mass, speed, energy) have size only and cannot be drawn this way.
Force examples are vectors: weight, friction, tension, drag, upthrust.

callouts.p: A **vector** quantity has both **magnitude and direction**; a **scalar** has magnitude only.

core.h: Friction and drag in more detail
core.p: Friction is a contact force that always **opposes motion** (or attempted motion) between surfaces. It transfers energy to the thermal store, heating the surfaces.
bullets: Rougher surfaces and a larger normal contact force give **more friction**.
Friction is useful for grip (tyres, shoes, brakes).
Friction is a problem when it wastes energy as heat in machines; **lubrication** reduces it.
**Drag** (air or water resistance) increases with **speed** and with **cross-sectional area**.
Streamlining reduces drag.

core.p: Non-contact forces act through fields, and the strength of a field decreases with distance from the object that produces it.
bullets: Gravitational force between two objects is **bigger for bigger masses** and **smaller at greater separation**.
Electrostatic force is **bigger for bigger charges** and **smaller at greater separation**.
Magnetic force is strongest **near the poles** and weakens with distance.
This is why satellites far from Earth feel a smaller gravitational force.

callouts.p: Write 'the further apart, the weaker the force' - examiners reward the direction of the relationship.

analogy.p: Two people pulling on either end of a rope are like two interacting objects: whatever force the rope exerts on one person, it exerts an equal and opposite force on the other, and both people feel it at the same moment. Non-contact forces are like an invisible rope stretched through a field - the objects still pull on each other without touching. The analogy breaks down because in real tug-of-war the people also push on the ground, which is why one team can win; and a field is not a physical rope, and it can repel as well as attract.

terms.d: A push or pull on an object arising from its interaction with another object, measured in newtons (N).
The unit of force.
A force that acts only when two objects are physically touching.
A force that acts between objects that are not touching, through a field.
The push of a surface on an object in contact with it, acting at 90 degrees to the surface.
A contact force that opposes the relative motion (or attempted motion) of two surfaces in contact.
A frictional force from air that opposes an object's motion and increases with speed.
The pulling force in a stretched string, rope or cable.
The upward force a fluid exerts on an object immersed in it.
An attractive non-contact force between any two objects that have mass.
The gravitational force on an object due to a planet; weight = mass x gravitational field strength.
A non-contact force between charged objects: like charges repel, unlike charges attract.
A non-contact force between magnets or magnetic materials: like poles repel, unlike poles attract.
A region in which an object experiences a non-contact force (gravitational, electric or magnetic).
Two forces of the same type, equal in size and opposite in direction, acting on two different interacting objects.
A quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as force.

mistakes.w: Weight and the normal contact force on a book form an interaction pair.
mistakes.r: They act on the **same object** and are different types; the pair of the weight is the **book pulling the Earth up**.

mistakes.w: The forces in an interaction pair cancel out.
mistakes.r: They act on **different objects**, so they **cannot cancel**.

mistakes.w: Gravity is a contact force because you are on the ground.
mistakes.r: Gravity is a **non-contact** force acting through a gravitational field.

mistakes.w: Magnets only attract.
mistakes.r: **Like poles repel, unlike poles attract**.

mistakes.w: The Earth does not feel a force from a falling apple.
mistakes.r: The apple pulls the Earth with an **equal** force; the Earth's huge mass means its acceleration is tiny.

mistakes.w: Normal contact force acts straight up.
mistakes.r: It acts **at 90 degrees to the surface** - on a slope it is not vertical.

mistakes.w: Friction always stops things moving.
mistakes.r: Friction **opposes relative motion**; it also lets you walk and grip.

mistakes.w: Mass and weight are the same thing.
mistakes.r: Mass (kg) is the amount of matter; **weight (N) is a force** = mass x g.

mistakes.w: One force in the pair happens first, then the reaction.
mistakes.r: Both forces act **at the same time**.

exam.q: Name two non-contact forces.
model: Any two from: gravitational force (weight)
electrostatic force / magnetic force
exam.tip: Air resistance is a contact force.

exam.q: State the unit of force.
model: newton (N)
exam.tip: Not kg.

exam.q: Explain the difference between a contact force and a non-contact force.
model: Contact force acts only when objects are touching
Non-contact force acts between objects that are not touching / through a field
exam.tip: Give a definition for each half.

exam.q: Classify each force as contact or non-contact: friction, magnetic force, tension, weight.
model: Contact: friction, tension
Non-contact: magnetic force, weight
exam.tip: Two correct = 1 mark, all four = 2 marks typically.

exam.q: A balloon rubbed on hair sticks to a wall. Name the type of force involved and state whether it is contact or non-contact.
model: Electrostatic force
Non-contact
exam.tip: Charged objects interact electrostatically.

exam.q: The Earth pulls a satellite with a gravitational force of 5000 N. Describe the other force in this interaction pair.
model: Gravitational force
of 5000 N
exerted by the satellite on the Earth, directed towards the satellite
exam.tip: Size, direction, type and which object it acts on.

exam.q: A student says that the weight of a cup and the normal contact force from the table on the cup are an interaction pair. Explain why the student is wrong.
model: Both forces act on the same object (the cup)
They are different types of force (gravitational and contact)
Forces in an interaction pair act on different objects and are the same type
exam.tip: Use the test: same type and different objects.

exam.q: Explain how a person is able to walk forwards, in terms of an interaction pair.
model: Foot pushes backwards on the ground (friction)
Ground pushes forwards on the foot with an equal force
This forward force on the person moves them forward
exam.tip: Name the direction of each force and what it acts on.

exam.q: Explain why an apple falls towards the Earth but the Earth does not noticeably move towards the apple, even though the forces are equal.
model: The forces on apple and Earth are equal and opposite
Earth has a much larger mass
So Earth's acceleration is far smaller (too small to detect)
exam.tip: Link force, mass and acceleration.

exam.q: A box rests on a ramp. Describe the forces acting on the box and identify the interaction pair partner of each one. In your answer refer to contact and non-contact forces.
model: Weight: non-contact gravitational force from Earth, acting vertically down
Its partner: box pulls Earth upwards with an equal gravitational force
Normal contact force from ramp, at 90 degrees to the ramp surface
Its partner: box pushes on ramp into the surface with equal contact force
Friction from ramp acts up the slope, parallel to surface, stopping it sliding
Its partner: box exerts equal friction on the ramp down the slope
exam.tip: Level of response: each force needs type, direction and its partner on the other object.

worked.q: A 2 kg book rests on a table on Earth (g = 9.8 N/kg). Identify both interaction pairs involving the book and give the size of each force.
steps: Weight of book = mg = 2 x 9.8 = 19.6 N downwards, Earth pulling on book
Pair 1 partner: book pulls Earth upwards with 19.6 N (gravitational)
The book is at rest, so the table pushes up on the book with 19.6 N (normal contact force)
Pair 2 partner: book pushes down on the table with 19.6 N (contact force)
worked.ans: Gravitational pair: 19.6 N on book (down) and 19.6 N on Earth (up). Contact pair: 19.6 N on book (up) and 19.6 N on table (down).

worked.q: Two ice skaters stand facing each other. Skater A pushes skater B with a force of 60 N. Describe what happens and why.
steps: Skater A pushes B with 60 N; by the interaction pair, B pushes A with 60 N in the opposite direction
Both forces are contact forces acting on different skaters at the same time
Both skaters move apart
The skater with the smaller mass moves away with the greater acceleration
worked.ans: Both skaters move apart because each feels a 60 N push; the lighter skater moves faster.

worked.q: Classify these interactions and state the force type: (a) a fridge magnet on a steel door (b) a car tyre on a road (c) the Moon and the Earth.
steps: (a) Magnetic force - non-contact (plus contact once touching)
(b) Friction and normal contact force - contact
(c) Gravitational force - non-contact
worked.ans: (a) magnetic, non-contact (b) friction / normal contact, contact (c) gravitational, non-contact

phy_ocra.4.1.summary: A **free body diagram** shows one object with every force acting on it drawn as a labelled arrow. Adding these forces as vectors gives the **resultant force** - the single force that has the same effect as all of them together. If the resultant force is zero the forces are **balanced** and the object is in **equilibrium**: it stays at rest or keeps moving at constant velocity. Higher tier students use **scale vector diagrams** to add forces at angles (tip to tail), to **resolve** a force into two perpendicular components, and to show equilibrium as a **closed triangle** of forces.

core.p: A **free body diagram** isolates one object and shows **only the forces acting on that object**, drawn as arrows starting from the object. It is the first step in working out what the object will do.
bullets: Draw the object as a simple **box or dot**.
Draw each force as an **arrow from the object** in the direction it acts.
Make **arrow length proportional to force size**.
**Label** each arrow with its name and size, e.g. weight 800 N.
Include **only forces on the object**, never forces the object exerts on other things.
Common forces: **weight** (down), **normal contact force** (at 90 degrees to surface), **friction/drag** (opposite to motion), **thrust/driving force** (forwards), **tension**, **upthrust**.

callouts.p: A **free body diagram** shows a single object and **all the forces acting on it**, each as a labelled arrow showing size and direction.

core.p: When several forces act on an object, their combined effect is the same as one single force: the **resultant force** (also called the **net force**). It is what decides whether the object's motion changes.
bullets: Forces in the **same direction**: **add** them.
Forces in **opposite directions**: **subtract** the smaller from the larger.
The resultant acts in the direction of the **larger** force.
Example: 50 N right and 20 N left gives a resultant of **30 N to the right**.
Choose one direction as **positive** to avoid sign mistakes.
A non-zero resultant force makes the object **accelerate** (speed up, slow down or change direction).

callouts.p: The **resultant force** is the **single force** that has the **same effect** as all the forces acting on an object combined.

core.p: If all the forces cancel, the resultant force is **zero** and the forces are **balanced**. The object is then in **equilibrium** and its velocity does not change.
bullets: Resultant force = 0 means **balanced forces**.
A stationary object **stays stationary**.
A moving object **keeps moving at constant velocity** (same speed, same direction).
Balanced does **not** mean stopped - a car cruising at a steady 30 m/s can have balanced forces.
Examples: a book resting on a table; a skydiver at **terminal velocity**; a hanging picture.
Forces on a stationary object in equilibrium balance **in every direction** (horizontally and vertically).

callouts.p: An object is in **equilibrium** when the **resultant force on it is zero**; the forces are **balanced**.

core.p: If the resultant force is **not zero**, the forces are **unbalanced** and the object accelerates in the direction of the resultant force.
bullets: Driving force bigger than drag: car **accelerates**.
Drag bigger than driving force: car **decelerates**.
Weight bigger than air resistance: a skydiver **speeds up** downwards.
A bigger resultant force gives a **bigger acceleration** for the same mass.
The acceleration is always in the **direction of the resultant force**, not necessarily the direction of motion.

callouts.p: An object does not need a resultant force to **keep** moving - only to **change** its velocity.

core.p: When forces act at an angle to each other you cannot just add or subtract their sizes. Instead you draw them as vectors to scale and add them **tip to tail**.
bullets: Choose a **sensible scale**, e.g. 1 cm = 10 N, and write it down.
Draw the first force arrow to scale in the correct direction using a **ruler and protractor**.
Draw the second force starting from the **tip (head) of the first** - **tip to tail**.
The **resultant** is the arrow from the **tail of the first** to the **tip of the last**.
Measure its **length** and convert with the scale to get the size; measure the **angle** for the direction.
Alternatively, use the **parallelogram method**: draw both forces from one point, complete the parallelogram, and the diagonal is the resultant.

callouts.p: Use a sharp pencil, a scale that makes the diagram large, and give the direction as an angle from a stated reference line.

core.p: When two forces are at **90 degrees**, the vector diagram is a right-angled triangle, so you can check a scale drawing with **Pythagoras** and trigonometry.
bullets: Size: **R = square root of (F1 squared + F2 squared)**.
Example: 30 N and 40 N at right angles: R = square root of (900 + 1600) = **50 N**.
Direction: **tan(angle) = opposite / adjacent**, e.g. tan(angle) = 40 / 30 gives 53 degrees.
The resultant of two forces is always **less than or equal to their sum** and **at least their difference**.
OCR accepts scale drawing answers within a tolerance; calculation gives a check.

core.p: **Resolving** is the reverse of adding: one force is split into **two perpendicular components** that together have the same effect. This helps you analyse forces on slopes or ropes pulling at an angle.
bullets: Draw the force to scale as the **diagonal of a rectangle** (or hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle).
Draw the **horizontal** and **vertical** sides; their lengths (with the scale) give the components.
For a force F at angle theta to the horizontal: horizontal component = **F cos theta**, vertical = **F sin theta** (useful check).
Example: 100 N at 30 degrees above horizontal: about **87 N horizontal** and **50 N vertical**.
On a slope, weight resolves into a component **down the slope** and a component **into the slope**.
Only the component **in the direction of motion** speeds the object up.

callouts.p: **Resolving** a force means splitting it into **two components at right angles** that together have the same effect as the original force.

core.p: If an object is in equilibrium, adding all the force vectors tip to tail brings you **back to the starting point**. The arrows form a **closed shape** - a closed triangle for three forces - and the resultant is zero.
bullets: Draw each force tip to tail in turn, to scale.
If the last arrow ends exactly where the first began, the forces are **balanced**.
If there is a gap, the arrow needed to close it is **equal and opposite** to the resultant.
Use this to find an **unknown force**: it is the side that closes the triangle.
Example: a picture hanging from two strings - the two tensions and the weight form a closed triangle.
For forces in equilibrium, horizontal components sum to zero **and** vertical components sum to zero.

callouts.p: Three forces in equilibrium form a **closed triangle** when drawn tip to tail: **resultant force = 0**.

core.h: Worked situations: everyday free body diagrams
core.p: Exam questions often describe a situation and ask you to draw or interpret the forces. Use the free body diagram to decide whether forces are balanced.
bullets: **Skydiver just after jumping**: weight much larger than air resistance, so resultant downwards, accelerating.
**Skydiver at terminal velocity**: weight = air resistance, resultant zero, constant velocity.
**Boat floating at rest**: weight = upthrust.
**Lift accelerating upwards**: tension in cable greater than weight.
**Box pushed at constant speed**: push = friction.
**Object on a slope at rest**: weight, normal contact force and friction form a closed triangle.

core.p: Clear diagrams earn marks; messy or incomplete ones lose them. Follow these rules every time.
bullets: Arrows start **on the object** (usually from its centre).
Balanced pairs of forces should have **equal-length arrows**.
Do not draw the resultant force on the same diagram unless asked (it is not an extra force).
Do not include forces that the object **exerts on** something else.
Weight always acts **vertically downwards**, from the centre of mass.

callouts.p: There is no 'force of motion' - a moving object keeps moving without a forward force if the forces are balanced.

analogy.p: Imagine several people pulling a heavy crate with ropes in different directions. The crate only cares about the overall pull - the resultant - as if one super-strong person pulled in a single direction. If the teams pull so that everything cancels, the crate stays still or keeps sliding steadily: equilibrium. Walking the ropes one after another, tip to tail, tells you where that single person would need to pull. The analogy breaks down because ropes can only pull (tension), while real forces can also push, and forces like gravity act without anything attached.

mistakes.w: Balanced forces mean the object is not moving.
mistakes.r: Balanced forces mean **no change in velocity** - the object is stationary **or** moving at **constant velocity**.

mistakes.w: Adding 30 N and 40 N at right angles gives 70 N.
mistakes.r: Use a **vector diagram** or Pythagoras: the resultant is **50 N**.

mistakes.w: Drawing forces the object exerts on other objects on a free body diagram.
mistakes.r: Show **only forces acting on** the chosen object.

mistakes.w: A moving object must have a resultant force in its direction of motion.
mistakes.r: A resultant force is needed only to **change** velocity.

mistakes.w: Resultant direction given as 'diagonal' or 'up and right'.
mistakes.r: Give the direction as an **angle measured from a stated reference** (e.g. 53 degrees above the horizontal).

mistakes.w: Joining vectors tail to tail when adding.
mistakes.r: Add vectors **tip to tail**; the resultant goes from the first tail to the last tip.

mistakes.w: No scale stated on a scale drawing.
mistakes.r: State the **scale** (e.g. 1 cm = 10 N) and make the diagram large.

mistakes.w: Normal contact force always drawn vertically upwards.
mistakes.r: Draw it **at 90 degrees to the surface**; on a slope it is tilted.

mistakes.w: Resultant force drawn as an extra force on the free body diagram.
mistakes.r: The resultant **replaces** the forces; it is not an additional force.

exam.q: State what is meant by the resultant force on an object.
model: The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on the object together
exam.tip: Use the words 'single force' and 'same effect'.

exam.q: An object has a resultant force of zero acting on it. Describe its possible motion.
model: Stays stationary if at rest
or moves at constant velocity / constant speed in a straight line
exam.tip: Both possibilities are needed for 2 marks.

exam.q: A box has a 70 N push to the right and 25 N of friction to the left. Calculate the resultant force.
model: to the right
exam.tip: Direction is part of the answer.

exam.q: Draw a free body diagram for a skydiver falling at terminal velocity.
model: Weight arrow downwards and air resistance arrow upwards
Arrows equal in length, labelled
exam.tip: Equal lengths show balanced forces.

exam.q: A boat is pulled by two ropes at right angles with forces of 600 N and 800 N. Calculate the size of the resultant force.
model: R squared = 600 squared + 800 squared
R = square root of 1 000 000
exam.tip: A scale drawing is also accepted if precise.

exam.q: Describe how to use a scale drawing to find the resultant of two forces acting at 60 degrees to each other.
model: Choose and state a suitable scale
Draw the first force to scale in the correct direction
Draw the second force from the tip of the first at the correct angle (tip to tail)
Draw the resultant from start to finish; measure length and angle and convert using scale
exam.tip: Mention ruler and protractor for precision.

exam.q: A force of 200 N acts at 40 degrees above the horizontal. Use a scale drawing or calculation to find its horizontal and vertical components.
model: Horizontal = 200 cos 40 = 153 N (about 150 N)
Vertical = 200 sin 40 = 129 N (about 130 N)
Correct method shown (scale rectangle or trigonometry)
exam.tip: Tolerances are allowed for scale drawings.

exam.q: A lamp hangs from two cables. Explain how a vector diagram can show that the lamp is in equilibrium.
model: Draw the two tensions and the weight to scale tip to tail
The arrows form a closed triangle
So the resultant force is zero (equilibrium)
exam.tip: 'Closed triangle' is the key phrase.

exam.q: A car of weight 10 000 N is driving at constant speed along a level road. The driving force is 2500 N. State the size of (a) the resistive forces and (b) the normal contact force, and explain your answers.
model: Constant velocity so resultant force is zero; forces balance horizontally and vertically
exam.tip: Constant speed in a straight line means equilibrium.

exam.q: A skydiver jumps from a plane, later opens a parachute and lands. Use free body diagrams and the idea of resultant force to explain how her velocity changes during the fall.
model: At first weight is much larger than air resistance, so resultant force is downwards and she accelerates
As speed increases, air resistance increases, so the resultant force decreases and acceleration decreases
When air resistance equals weight the resultant is zero and she reaches terminal velocity
Parachute opens: air resistance becomes larger than weight, resultant is upwards, she decelerates
As she slows, air resistance falls until it equals weight again
She reaches a new, lower terminal velocity before landing
exam.tip: Level of response: describe the forces AND the resulting motion at each stage.

worked.q: A crate has four forces on it: 500 N up, 500 N down, 180 N to the right and 60 N to the left. Find the resultant force and describe the crate's motion if it starts at rest.
steps: Vertical: 500 - 500 = 0 N, so balanced vertically
Horizontal: 180 - 60 = 120 N to the right
Resultant = 120 N to the right
Resultant is not zero, so the crate accelerates to the right
worked.ans: 120 N to the right; the crate starts moving and accelerates to the right.

worked.q: A tug pulls a ship east with 4000 N while the wind pushes it north with 3000 N. Find the resultant force and its direction.
steps: Forces at right angles, so R = square root of (4000 squared + 3000 squared)
R = square root of (16 000 000 + 9 000 000) = square root of 25 000 000 = 5000 N
tan(angle) = 3000 / 4000 = 0.75, angle = 37 degrees
Direction: 37 degrees north of east
worked.ans: 5000 N at 37 degrees north of east

worked.q: A child pulls a sledge with a rope at 30 degrees to the horizontal with a force of 60 N. The sledge moves at constant velocity. Find the friction force.
steps: Resolve the 60 N: horizontal component = 60 cos 30 = 52 N
Vertical component = 60 sin 30 = 30 N (reduces the normal contact force)
Constant velocity so horizontal forces are balanced
Friction = horizontal component of pull
worked.ans: Friction = 52 N opposing the motion

phy_ocra.4.2.summary: Newton's first law says that if the **resultant force** on an object is zero, its velocity does not change: a stationary object stays still and a moving object keeps the same speed in the same direction. Any change in speed or direction needs a non-zero resultant force. A falling object speeds up until the **drag** (air resistance) grows to equal its **weight**; the resultant force is then zero, so by the first law it falls at a constant **terminal velocity**. You can investigate this in PAG P3 by timing objects falling through a fluid or through air.

core.p: Newton's first law describes what happens when the forces on an object are **balanced**, meaning the **resultant force is zero**. It applies to objects that are not moving and to objects that are already moving.
bullets: If the resultant force on a **stationary** object is zero, it **remains stationary**.
If the resultant force on a **moving** object is zero, it **continues to move at the same speed in the same direction** (constant velocity).
Objects do NOT need a force to keep moving. They need a resultant force only to **change** their motion.
Constant velocity and being at rest are both examples of **equilibrium**.
The law is really a statement about velocity: zero resultant force means **zero acceleration**.

callouts.p: If the resultant force acting on an object is zero, the object will remain at rest, or if it is moving it will continue to move at the same speed in the same direction (at constant velocity).

callouts.t: Moving does not mean a force is winning
callouts.p: A car cruising at a steady 30 m/s has balanced forces. Do not write that the driving force is bigger than the friction.

core.h: What a non-zero resultant force does
core.p: The flip side of the first law: if the resultant force is **not zero**, the velocity **must change**. Velocity is a vector, so a change can be a change of speed, a change of direction, or both.
bullets: Resultant force **in the direction of motion**: the object **speeds up** (accelerates).
Resultant force **opposite to the motion**: the object **slows down** (decelerates).
Resultant force **at an angle** to the motion: the object **changes direction**.
An object moving in a circle at constant speed is still accelerating because its direction keeps changing, so there must be a resultant force.
The bigger the resultant force, the quicker the velocity changes (linked to F = ma, covered in the next point).

callouts.p: Changing direction counts as changing velocity, so turning always needs a resultant force even if the speedometer reading stays the same.

core.h: Applying the first law to vehicles
core.p: A vehicle has a **driving force** (from the engine, via friction between tyres and road) forwards and **resistive forces** (air resistance and friction) backwards. Comparing them tells you how the vehicle moves.
bullets: Driving force **greater than** resistive forces: resultant forwards, car **accelerates**.
Driving force **equal to** resistive forces: resultant zero, car moves at **constant velocity**.
Driving force **less than** resistive forces (for example when braking): resultant backwards, car **decelerates**.
Air resistance **increases with speed**, so a car with a fixed maximum driving force reaches a **top speed** when air resistance plus friction equals that driving force.
Vertical forces (weight down, normal contact force up) are balanced too, so the car does not accelerate up or down.

callouts.p: In explanations always name both forces and compare them, for example: the driving force equals the total resistive force, so the resultant force is zero.

core.h: Weight and drag on a falling object
core.p: Two forces act on an object falling through air (or any fluid): its **weight** downwards, which stays constant, and **drag** (air resistance) upwards, which **depends on speed**.
bullets: **Weight** = mass x gravitational field strength (W = mg). On Earth g is about 10 N/kg, so weight does not change during the fall.
**Drag** acts **opposite to the direction of motion**, so for a falling object it acts upwards.
Drag **increases as speed increases**, because the object collides with more fluid particles each second, and harder.
Drag also increases with a larger **cross-sectional area** (more streamlined shapes have less drag).
Drag is larger in a more **viscous** or denser fluid: much larger in oil or water than in air.

head: Factor
Effect on drag
Effect on terminal velocity
rows: (this is why terminal velocity is reached)
More drag at a given speed
Higher terminal velocity (more drag needed to balance)
More drag at a given speed

callouts.p: During a fall the weight stays the same; it is the drag that grows with speed. That change is what causes terminal velocity.

core.h: Reaching terminal velocity step by step
core.p: Terminal velocity is a direct use of Newton's first law. The chain of reasoning below is exactly what a 6 mark answer needs, in this order.
bullets: At the very start the speed is zero, so **drag is zero**; the only force is weight, so the resultant force is downwards and the object **accelerates** at g (about 10 m/s squared).
As the speed increases, **drag increases**.
The **resultant force (weight minus drag) decreases**, so the **acceleration decreases**; the object still speeds up, but more slowly.
Eventually **drag equals weight**: the forces are balanced and the **resultant force is zero**.
By Newton's first law the object now moves at a **constant velocity**: the **terminal velocity**.
The object does NOT stop accelerating suddenly; the acceleration falls gradually towards zero.

callouts.p: The maximum, constant velocity reached by a falling object when the drag (air resistance) acting on it is equal to its weight, so the resultant force is zero.
Before terminal velocity the object is still speeding up. Its acceleration is getting smaller, which is different from slowing down.

core.p: The skydiver is the classic exam context. Compare the size of weight and drag at each stage and use the first law.
bullets: **Just after jumping**: weight is much greater than drag, large downward resultant, large acceleration.
**Falling faster**: drag grows, resultant force and acceleration decrease.
**First terminal velocity** (roughly 50 to 60 m/s): drag = weight, resultant zero, constant velocity.

**Parachute opens**: the much larger surface area means drag suddenly becomes **greater than** weight; the resultant force is **upwards**, so the skydiver **decelerates** (slows down) while still moving downwards.
As the skydiver slows, drag **decreases** until it again equals weight; a new, **lower terminal velocity** (a few m/s) is reached, which is safe for landing.
On landing, the ground exerts a large upward force that brings the skydiver to rest.

callouts.t: The skydiver does not go up
callouts.p: When the parachute opens the resultant force is upwards but the skydiver keeps moving downwards, just more slowly. Film footage only looks as if they rise because the camera person is still falling fast.

core.h: Velocity-time graph for a falling object
core.p: The shape of the velocity-time graph shows the changing acceleration, because the **gradient of a velocity-time graph equals the acceleration**.
bullets: At the start the graph is **steepest**: largest acceleration (about 10 m/s squared, when drag is zero).
The gradient **gradually decreases** as drag increases: acceleration decreasing.
The graph becomes **horizontal** (gradient zero) at terminal velocity: zero acceleration, zero resultant force.
When the parachute opens the graph drops steeply: a **large deceleration**.
It levels off again at a **lower** horizontal line: the second terminal velocity.
The area under the graph is the distance fallen.

callouts.p: Draw a smooth curve that bends over into a flat line. Do not draw a sharp corner where terminal velocity is reached: the acceleration decreases gradually.

core.h: Why a parachute gives a lower terminal velocity
core.p: Opening the parachute does not change the weight. It changes how much drag there is at each speed.
bullets: The parachute has a **much larger surface area**, so it collides with far more air particles each second.
At the same speed, the drag is therefore much larger than before.
To balance the same weight, the drag only needs to reach the weight value, which now happens at a **much lower speed**.
So the **second terminal velocity is lower** than the first.
Heavier skydivers (or objects with greater weight) have a **higher** terminal velocity, because drag must grow larger to balance their weight.

callouts.t: Same weight, more drag per m/s
callouts.p: Terminal velocity is lower with the parachute because the same drag force (equal to the weight) is produced at a lower speed.

core.h: Terminal velocity in liquids and for vehicles
core.p: The same reasoning applies whenever a resistive force grows with speed.
bullets: A ball bearing dropped into **oil or glycerol** reaches terminal velocity within a few centimetres because the drag from a viscous liquid is large.
Raindrops and hailstones reach terminal velocity long before hitting the ground.
A car's **top speed** is a terminal velocity: maximum driving force = air resistance + friction.
Cyclists and racing cars use **streamlined shapes** to reduce drag and so increase their top speed.
Some animals and seeds (for example sycamore seeds) have large surface areas so they fall slowly.

callouts.p: If a question uses an unfamiliar object (a feather, a seed, a ball in oil), apply the same chain: drag increases with speed until it equals the weight, so resultant force is zero and velocity is constant.

core.p: A common practical is dropping objects through a fluid and measuring how their speed changes. One version uses a ball bearing in a tall tube of oil or glycerol; another uses paper cake cases falling through air.
bullets: **Tube method**: place rubber bands round a tall tube of glycerol at equal intervals (for example every 10 cm). Drop a ball bearing in and use a stopwatch (or video) to time how long it takes to pass between each pair of bands.
When the **times between equally spaced bands become equal**, the ball has reached **terminal velocity**.
Terminal velocity = **distance between bands / time between bands**.
Place the first band a little below the surface so the ball is not timed while still accelerating from rest.
**Cake case method**: drop paper cake cases from a fixed height; stack cases to increase the weight while keeping the shape and area the same. Time the fall over the lower part of the drop.
**Independent variable**: mass (number of cases or size of ball bearing). **Dependent variable**: terminal velocity. **Control variables**: shape, cross-sectional area, fluid, drop height.
Use a **video camera with a metre rule** or **light gates** to reduce reaction time errors; repeat and calculate a mean; read the bands at eye level to avoid parallax.

head: Problem
Improvement
rows: Use video analysis or light gates
Start timing lower down the tube
Keep eye level with each band

callouts.p: The examiner wants: equal times for equal distances, so the speed is constant.

core.h: Linking to equilibrium and other points
core.p: The first law ties together several ideas you will meet across this topic.
bullets: An object at rest or at constant velocity is in **equilibrium**: the vector sum of the forces is zero.
The tendency of an object to keep doing what it is doing (stay at rest or keep moving) is called **inertia**.
If the resultant is not zero, Newton's second law (F = ma) tells you how big the acceleration is.
A **free body diagram** with arrows drawn to scale shows at a glance whether forces are balanced.
Forces are only balanced if they act **on the same object**; this is different from a Newton's third law pair, which acts on two different objects.

callouts.t: Balanced is not the same as third-law pair
callouts.p: Weight and drag on a skydiver at terminal velocity are balanced forces on one object. They are not a Newton's third law pair.

analogy.p: Imagine pedalling a bike with the same effort at all times, while a magic headwind blows harder the faster you go. At first you gain speed quickly, then more slowly as the headwind builds, until the headwind pushes back exactly as hard as you push forward and your speed stays steady. Your constant effort is like weight, and the headwind is like drag. The analogy breaks down because real drag is caused by the object moving through still air, not by wind, and a skydiver does not pedal: the weight is supplied by gravity and needs no effort at all.

mistakes.w: A car moving at constant speed has a bigger forward force than backward force.
mistakes.r: At constant velocity the driving force equals the resistive forces, so the resultant force is zero.

mistakes.w: At terminal velocity there are no forces acting on the skydiver.
mistakes.r: Weight and drag still act; they are equal and opposite, so the resultant force is zero.

mistakes.w: The skydiver's weight decreases as they fall, so they stop accelerating.
mistakes.r: Weight stays constant; the drag increases with speed until it equals the weight.

mistakes.w: When the parachute opens the skydiver moves upwards.
mistakes.r: The resultant force is upwards so the skydiver decelerates, but they keep moving downwards.

mistakes.w: The parachute increases the skydiver's weight / reduces gravity.
mistakes.r: The parachute increases surface area, so drag increases at a given speed; weight is unchanged.

mistakes.w: Before terminal velocity the skydiver is decelerating because the acceleration is decreasing.
mistakes.r: The skydiver is still speeding up; the acceleration decreases because the resultant force decreases.

mistakes.w: Drag increases because the skydiver gets closer to the ground.
mistakes.r: Drag increases because the speed increases.

mistakes.w: Terminal velocity is when the object reaches the ground.
mistakes.r: Terminal velocity is the constant velocity when drag equals weight, reached during the fall.

mistakes.w: An object moving in a circle at constant speed has no resultant force.
mistakes.r: Its direction is changing, so its velocity changes and there must be a resultant force.

exam.q: State Newton's first law of motion.
model: If the resultant force on an object is zero
it stays at rest, or keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction (constant velocity)
exam.tip: Say 'resultant force is zero', not 'no forces act'.

exam.q: A lorry travels along a straight, level road at a constant speed. The driving force is 4500 N. What is the total resistive force on the lorry?
exam.tip: Constant velocity means balanced forces.

exam.q: Explain why a car driving with its maximum engine force eventually reaches a top speed.
model: Air resistance increases as the speed increases
eventually resistive forces equal the driving force
resultant force is zero so the car moves at constant velocity (no further acceleration)
exam.tip: Mention what changes (air resistance) and why it matters (resultant force).

exam.q: A skydiver jumps from a plane. Explain why she accelerates at first.
model: At the start drag (air resistance) is zero or very small
so weight is greater than drag and there is a downward resultant force
exam.tip: Always compare the two forces.

exam.q: Describe and explain the motion of a skydiver from leaving the plane until reaching terminal velocity, before the parachute opens.
model: At first the only significant force is weight, so she accelerates downwards (at about 10 m/s squared)
As speed increases, air resistance increases
Weight stays the same
Resultant force (weight minus drag) decreases
So the acceleration decreases, but she is still speeding up
Eventually air resistance equals weight, resultant force is zero, and she falls at constant velocity: terminal velocity (Newton's first law)
exam.tip: Write it as a logical chain; each link scores a mark.

exam.q: Explain why the skydiver slows down when she opens her parachute and why she then reaches a new terminal velocity.
model: The parachute increases surface area so air resistance increases
Air resistance becomes greater than weight, so the resultant force is upwards and she decelerates
As she slows down, air resistance decreases
When air resistance equals weight again she reaches a new, lower terminal velocity
exam.tip: Say 'resultant force upwards' and 'decelerates'; never say she moves up.

exam.q: Sketch a velocity-time graph for a skydiver from leaving the plane to landing, and label the point where terminal velocity is first reached.
model: Curve starting at origin with decreasing gradient
Levelling off to a horizontal line labelled terminal velocity
Steep drop when parachute opens, levelling to a lower horizontal line
exam.tip: The gradient must change smoothly, not abruptly.

exam.q: A student drops a ball bearing into a tube of glycerol. Rubber bands are placed every 10 cm. The times between bands are 0.62 s, 0.51 s, 0.48 s, 0.48 s, 0.48 s. Explain how the data show the ball reached terminal velocity and calculate it.
model: The time for each 10 cm becomes constant (0.48 s)
so the ball travels equal distances in equal times: constant speed
speed = distance / time = 0.10 / 0.48
exam.tip: Convert cm to m before dividing.

exam.q: Suggest two improvements to the method of the student in the previous question.
model: Use video recording or light gates instead of a stopwatch to reduce reaction time error
Repeat the drops and calculate a mean (or keep eye level with bands to avoid parallax)
exam.tip: Link each improvement to the error it reduces.

exam.q: Two balls of the same size but different mass are dropped from a high building. Explain which reaches the higher terminal velocity.
model: The heavier ball has a greater weight
Air resistance on the heavier ball must become larger to balance its weight
Drag increases with speed, so it must fall faster: higher terminal velocity
exam.tip: Same size means same drag at the same speed; weight is the difference.

exam.q: A satellite orbits Earth at constant speed. Explain why there must be a resultant force on it.
model: Its direction of motion is continuously changing, so its velocity is changing
A change in velocity requires a resultant force (Newton's first law)
exam.tip: Velocity is a vector: direction matters.

worked.q: A skydiver of mass 80 kg falls through the air. Take g = 10 N/kg. (a) Calculate her weight. (b) At one moment the air resistance is 300 N. Calculate the resultant force. (c) What is the air resistance at terminal velocity?
steps: Weight = mass x gravitational field strength = 80 x 10 = 800 N
Resultant force = weight - air resistance = 800 - 300 = 500 N downwards
At terminal velocity the resultant force is zero, so air resistance = weight
worked.ans: (a) 800 N (b) 500 N downwards (c) 800 N

worked.q: A car travels at a constant 25 m/s on a straight road. The air resistance is 1200 N and the friction from the road and bearings is 600 N. What driving force does the engine provide? What happens if the driver increases the driving force to 2500 N?
steps: Constant velocity, so by Newton's first law the resultant force is zero
Total resistive force = 1200 + 600 = 1800 N
Driving force = 1800 N
With 2500 N driving force the resultant is 2500 - 1800 = 700 N forwards, so the car accelerates
As speed rises, air resistance increases until total resistance is 2500 N, giving a new, higher constant speed
worked.ans: 1800 N; the car accelerates, then reaches a new higher constant speed.

worked.q: In PAG P3 a cake case falls the last 1.20 m of its drop in 0.80 s at constant speed. Calculate its terminal velocity. Predict what happens if three cases are stacked together.
steps: Terminal velocity = distance / time = 1.20 / 0.80
Stacking cases keeps the shape and area the same but increases the weight
Drag must be larger to balance the larger weight, so the cases must fall faster before drag equals weight
worked.ans: 1.5 m/s; the stacked cases reach a higher terminal velocity.

phy_ocra.4.3.summary: Newton's second law says that the **acceleration** of an object is **directly proportional to the resultant force** on it and **inversely proportional to its mass**. This is written as **force = mass x acceleration (F = ma)**, with force in newtons, mass in kilograms and acceleration in m/s squared. The acceleration is always in the **same direction as the resultant force**. In PAG P2 you test this by pulling a trolley with different forces and measuring its acceleration with light gates.

core.h: The statement of Newton's second law
core.p: The first law says what happens when the resultant force is zero. The second law tells you **how much** an object accelerates when the resultant force is not zero.
bullets: The acceleration of an object is **directly proportional to the resultant force** acting on it: double the force, double the acceleration (for the same mass).
The acceleration is **inversely proportional to the mass** of the object: double the mass, half the acceleration (for the same force).
Combined into one equation: **resultant force = mass x acceleration**.
The acceleration is in the **same direction** as the resultant force.
It is the **resultant** force that matters, not any single force on the object.

callouts.p: The acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force acting on it, and inversely proportional to the mass of the object: resultant force = mass x acceleration.
force (N) = mass (kg) x acceleration (m/s squared), F = m x a. You must recall this; it is not given on the equation sheet.

core.p: The equation also defines the unit of force. Using SI units throughout makes the numbers work with no extra factors.
bullets: Force F in **newtons (N)**.
Mass m in **kilograms (kg)**: convert grams by dividing by 1000 (250 g = 0.25 kg).
Acceleration a in **metres per second squared (m/s squared)**.
**1 newton** is the force needed to give a mass of **1 kg** an acceleration of **1 m/s squared**.
So 1 N = 1 kg m/s squared.

callouts.p: One newton is the resultant force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s squared.
Using a mass in grams gives an answer 1000 times too big. Always convert to kg first.

core.p: Exams ask for any one of the three quantities. Rearrange before substituting.
bullets: **F = m x a** to find the resultant force.
**a = F / m** to find the acceleration.
**m = F / a** to find the mass.
Write the equation, substitute with units, then give the answer with a unit.
Show working: a correct method earns marks even if the final number slips.

callouts.p: Put F on top and m and a underneath. Cover the quantity you want to see the rearranged equation.

core.p: Most real objects have several forces on them. You must first combine them into the resultant force, then use F = ma.
bullets: Forces in the **same direction add**; forces in **opposite directions subtract**.
For a car: resultant force = driving force - (air resistance + friction).
For a rocket lifting off: resultant force = thrust - weight (- air resistance).
For a falling object: resultant force = weight - drag.
If the resultant comes out negative in your chosen direction, the acceleration is in the opposite direction (deceleration).

callouts.p: Using the driving force or thrust alone in F = ma instead of the resultant force.

core.p: Force and acceleration are both **vectors**, so direction matters.
bullets: The acceleration is always in the direction of the **resultant force**, which need not be the direction of motion.
If the resultant force is **opposite** to the motion, the object **decelerates**: its acceleration is negative.
A braking car has a resultant force backwards; a = F / m gives the size of the deceleration.
If the resultant force is at right angles to the motion, the object changes direction (as in circular motion).
Use a sign convention: pick one direction as positive and give forces in the other direction a minus sign.

callouts.p: If you calculate a = -4 m/s squared, state it as a deceleration of 4 m/s squared, or give the direction.

core.h: Proportionality: what the graphs look like
core.p: The second law predicts two simple relationships that you can test and recognise from graphs.
bullets: **Constant mass**: a graph of acceleration against resultant force is a **straight line through the origin**: a is directly proportional to F.
The **gradient** of the a against F graph equals **1 / m**, so a steeper line means a **smaller mass**.
**Constant force**: acceleration decreases as mass increases; a graph of a against m is a curve, while a against 1/m is a straight line through the origin.
If the line does not pass through the origin (it cuts the force axis), friction is acting: a small force is needed before the trolley accelerates at all.
Equal increases in force give equal increases in acceleration.

callouts.p: To claim direct proportion you need a straight line AND it must pass through the origin.

core.h: Required practical PAG P2: force and acceleration
core.p: A trolley on a bench (or runway) is pulled by a string that runs over a pulley to a hanging mass. The weight of the hanging masses provides the accelerating force.
bullets: Attach a **card (interrupt card)** of known length to the trolley and set up **two light gates** connected to a data logger.
Each light gate measures the speed: **speed = card length / time the card blocks the beam**.
Acceleration = **(final speed - initial speed) / time between gates**. Some data loggers calculate this directly.

**Independent variable**: the accelerating force (weight of hanging masses, W = mg). **Dependent variable**: acceleration. **Control variables**: total mass being accelerated, the same runway and surface.
Keep the **total mass constant** by moving slotted masses from the trolley to the hanger, because the hanging mass is also being accelerated.
Repeat each force, calculate a mean, and plot acceleration against force.
For the mass investigation, keep the force constant and add masses to the trolley; acceleration decreases as mass increases.

head: Issue
How to deal with it
rows: Tilt the runway slightly until the trolley rolls at constant speed when pushed
Move masses from trolley to hanger so total mass is constant
Use light gates and a data logger
Use a buffer or catch box; keep feet clear of falling masses

callouts.p: Light gates remove human reaction time, so times are more accurate and the results more repeatable.

core.p: Turning raw light-gate readings into a conclusion is a common 4 to 6 mark question.
bullets: Calculate speed at each gate: card length (in m) / time (in s).
Calculate acceleration: change in speed / time between gates.
Plot **acceleration (y-axis) against force (x-axis)** with a line of best fit.
A straight line through the origin supports **a is proportional to F**, as Newton's second law predicts.
The gradient gives 1 / total mass, so total mass = 1 / gradient: a useful check on your results.
Anomalous points should be identified, repeated if possible, and left out of the mean and the line of best fit.

callouts.p: As the force increases the acceleration increases; the straight line through the origin shows acceleration is directly proportional to force (for constant mass).

core.h: Weight as a special case of F = ma
core.p: When the only force on an object is its weight, the second law gives the acceleration due to gravity.
bullets: Weight W = m x g, where g is gravitational field strength (about 10 N/kg on Earth).
In free fall, F = W = m g, so a = F / m = m g / m = g.
So all objects in free fall (no air resistance) accelerate at the **same rate**, about 10 m/s squared, whatever their mass.
A heavier object has more weight, but also more mass to accelerate; the two effects cancel.
With air resistance, the resultant is W - drag, so the acceleration is less than g.

callouts.p: Gravitational field strength in N/kg is numerically the same as free-fall acceleration in m/s squared.

core.p: OCR expects you to estimate the size of forces using typical masses and accelerations, then use F = ma.
bullets: Typical masses: person about 70 kg, car about 1000 to 1500 kg, lorry over 10 000 kg.
A family car can accelerate at roughly 2 to 3 m/s squared; hard braking gives a deceleration of roughly 5 to 7 m/s squared.
Braking force on a 1000 kg car decelerating at 6 m/s squared: F = 1000 x 6 = 6000 N.
Large decelerations (for example in a crash) need very large forces, which is why they cause injury.
Round sensibly: estimates should be given to 1 or 2 significant figures.

callouts.p: State the value you are assuming, for example 'mass of car about 1000 kg', so the examiner can follow your estimate.

core.h: Combining F = ma with motion equations
core.p: Many questions need two steps: find the acceleration from motion data, then the force (or the reverse).
bullets: acceleration = change in velocity / time, a = (v - u) / t.
Then F = m x a gives the resultant force.
Or find a from F / m, then use v = u + a t (or v squared - u squared = 2 a s on the equation sheet) to find speeds or distances.
Keep track of signs: a slowing object has a negative acceleration and a backward resultant force.
Always check the answer is sensible for the situation.

callouts.p: Convert minutes to seconds and km/h to m/s before calculating acceleration.

analogy.p: Push an empty supermarket trolley and it shoots off; push a full one with the same effort and it barely speeds up. Push the full one twice as hard and it speeds up twice as quickly. Your push is the resultant force, the load is the mass, and how quickly it gains speed is the acceleration. The analogy breaks down because a real trolley has friction, so the resultant force is less than your push, and a person's 'effort' is not the same as a measured force in newtons.

terms.d: The acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force on it and inversely proportional to its mass.
The single force with the same effect as all the forces on an object combined.
The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms; it determines how hard the object is to accelerate.

mistakes.r: Use the resultant force: driving force minus the resistive forces.

mistakes.w: Using mass in grams, for example F = 500 x 2.
mistakes.r: Convert to kilograms first: 500 g = 0.5 kg, so F = 0.5 x 2 = 1 N.

mistakes.w: The bigger the mass, the bigger the acceleration.
mistakes.r: For the same force, a larger mass has a smaller acceleration (inversely proportional).

mistakes.w: A straight line graph shows the variables are directly proportional.
mistakes.r: It must be a straight line that passes through the origin.

mistakes.w: Acceleration unit written as m/s.
mistakes.r: Acceleration is in m/s squared (m/s2).

mistakes.w: Heavier objects fall faster in a vacuum because they have more weight.
mistakes.r: Weight and mass increase together, so a = W / m = g is the same for all objects.

mistakes.w: In PAG P2 the student adds masses to the hanger from a separate pile.
mistakes.r: Move masses from the trolley to the hanger so the total accelerated mass stays constant.

mistakes.w: The acceleration is always in the direction the object is moving.
mistakes.r: The acceleration is in the direction of the resultant force, which may oppose the motion.

exam.q: Write down the equation that links force, mass and acceleration.
model: force = mass x acceleration (F = m a)
exam.tip: Words or standard symbols both score.

exam.q: A resultant force of 24 N acts on a 6 kg box. Calculate its acceleration.
model: = 4 m/s squared
exam.tip: Give the unit.

exam.q: A car of mass 1200 kg has a driving force of 3000 N and resistive forces of 600 N. Calculate its acceleration.

= 2 m/s squared
exam.tip: Find the resultant before using F = ma.

exam.q: A trolley accelerates at 0.6 m/s squared when the resultant force is 1.5 N. Calculate the mass of the trolley.
exam.tip: Rearrange first, then substitute.

= 160 m/s squared

exam.q: Define one newton.
model: The force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s squared

exam.q: Describe how a student could investigate how the acceleration of a trolley depends on the force acting on it. Include how they would make it a fair test and how they would analyse the results.
model: Trolley on runway pulled by string over a pulley attached to hanging masses
Force = weight of hanging masses (W = m g)
Card on trolley passes through two light gates; speed = card length / time at each gate
Acceleration = change in speed / time between gates
Keep total mass constant by moving masses from trolley to hanger; same runway; compensate for friction by tilting runway

exam.tip: Cover equipment, measurements, calculations, control and analysis.

exam.q: In the investigation the graph of acceleration against force is a straight line that does not pass through the origin; it cuts the force axis. Suggest a reason.
model: Friction acts on the trolley
so a small force is needed to overcome friction before the trolley accelerates
exam.tip: Link the intercept to an extra force.

exam.q: A van of mass 2000 kg slows from 15 m/s to 5 m/s in 4 s. Calculate the braking force.
model: a = -2.5 m/s squared (deceleration of 2.5 m/s squared)
= 5000 N (opposite to motion)
exam.tip: Two-step: acceleration first, then force.

exam.q: Explain why a loaded lorry takes longer to reach 20 m/s than the same lorry when empty, if the resultant force is the same.
model: The loaded lorry has a larger mass
so for the same resultant force its acceleration is smaller (a = F / m), so it takes longer
exam.tip: Quote the relationship.

exam.q: Estimate the resultant force needed for a sprinter to accelerate from rest at the start of a race.
model: Assume mass about 70 kg
Assume acceleration about 4 to 5 m/s squared (any sensible value)

exam.tip: State your assumed values clearly.

worked.q: A rocket of mass 50 000 kg has an engine thrust of 800 000 N at lift-off. Take g = 10 N/kg. Ignore air resistance. Calculate its acceleration.

Resultant force = thrust - weight = 800 000 - 500 000 = 300 000 N upwards
a = 6 m/s squared upwards
worked.ans: 6 m/s squared upwards

worked.q: A cyclist and bike have a total mass of 90 kg. They slow from 12 m/s to 3 m/s in 3.0 s. Calculate the resultant force.

steps: Speed at gate 1 = 0.05 / 0.10 = 0.50 m/s
Speed at gate 2 = 0.05 / 0.025 = 2.0 m/s
worked.ans: a = 2.0 m/s squared; resultant force = 1.6 N

phy_ocra.4.4.summary: **Inertia** is the tendency of every object to stay at rest or to keep moving with the same velocity unless a resultant force acts on it; it is the idea behind Newton's first law. **Inertial mass** is a measure of **how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object**, including starting it moving from rest. It is defined as the **ratio of force over acceleration**, inertial mass = F / a, so a larger inertial mass means a smaller acceleration for the same resultant force. Inertia explains why passengers lurch forward when a car brakes and why heavy lorries are hard to start and stop.

core.p: Every object resists changes to its motion. This resistance is called **inertia**. It is not a force: it is a property of the object that depends on its mass.
bullets: An object at rest **tends to stay at rest**.
A moving object **tends to keep moving** at the same speed in the same direction.
To change either of these, a **resultant force** is needed (Newton's first law).
The more **mass** an object has, the more inertia it has.
Inertia applies everywhere, including in space where things are weightless.

callouts.p: The tendency of an object to continue in its state of rest or of uniform motion (constant velocity) unless acted on by a resultant force.
Do not draw inertia as an arrow on a free body diagram, and never write 'the force of inertia pushed the passenger forward'.

core.p: Inertial mass puts a number on inertia. It tells you how hard it is to change an object's velocity.
bullets: **Inertial mass** is a measure of **how difficult it is to change the velocity** of an object, including from rest.
It is defined as **inertial mass = force / acceleration** (m = F / a).
Unit: **kilogram (kg)**, because N / (m/s squared) = kg.
A **large** inertial mass means a **small** acceleration for a given resultant force.
This is just Newton's second law rearranged: F = m a, so m = F / a.

callouts.p: A measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object, defined as the ratio of force over acceleration: inertial mass = force / acceleration.
Inertial mass is the ratio F / a. Whatever force you apply, the ratio of that force to the acceleration it causes is the same for a given object.

core.p: The clearest way to see inertial mass is to apply the same resultant force to two objects and compare the accelerations.
bullets: A 10 N resultant force on a 1 kg trolley gives a = 10 / 1 = 10 m/s squared.
The same 10 N on a 5 kg trolley gives a = 10 / 5 = 2 m/s squared.
The 5 kg trolley has **five times the inertial mass**, so its velocity changes five times more slowly.
Acceleration is **inversely proportional** to inertial mass for a fixed force.
So a large inertial mass makes an object both **hard to start** and **hard to stop**.

callouts.p: If a question gives the force and acceleration for two objects, calculate F / a for each and compare. The larger ratio means more inertial mass.

core.p: Because inertial mass = F / a, you can measure it by applying known forces and measuring the accelerations, for example with the trolley, pulley and light gate set-up used for Newton's second law.
bullets: Apply a known resultant force (for example the weight of hanging masses).
Measure the acceleration with light gates or a data logger.
Repeat for several different forces.
Plot **force (y-axis) against acceleration (x-axis)**: the graph is a straight line through the origin.
The **gradient = F / a = inertial mass**.
Equivalently, on an acceleration against force graph the gradient is 1 / inertial mass.

callouts.p: Always check which quantity is on which axis before you say what the gradient represents.

core.p: Car safety features exist because of inertia. In a sudden stop the car decelerates, but the people inside tend to carry on moving.
bullets: When a car **brakes hard**, the braking force acts on the car, not directly on the passengers.
Because of their inertia, the passengers **continue moving forward** at the original speed.
The **seat belt** provides the backward force that decelerates the passenger with the car.
**Headrests** protect against whiplash: in a rear-end collision the car (and seat) is pushed forwards; the head tends to stay where it is until the headrest pushes it.
Unsecured objects (bags, phones) keep moving forward in a crash and can injure people.
A heavily loaded lorry has a large inertial mass, so it needs a much larger braking force or a longer distance to stop.

callouts.p: Passengers are not pushed forward by a force when a car brakes. They keep moving forward while the car slows down underneath them.
