core.p: Many familiar effects are explained by objects tending to keep their state of motion.
bullets: **Tablecloth trick**: pulled quickly, the cloth moves but the plates, with their inertia, stay almost still because the friction acts for only a very short time.
**Coin on a card over a glass**: flick the card away and the coin drops into the glass instead of moving with the card.
Standing passengers on a bus **lurch backwards** when the bus suddenly accelerates: their bodies tend to stay at rest while the bus moves forward.
Shaking water off your hands: your hands stop, but the drops carry on moving.
A hammer head can be tightened by banging the handle down: the handle stops, the head keeps moving down onto it.

callouts.p: Use the structure: the object was at rest (or moving); because of its inertia it tends to stay that way; the force on it was too small or too brief to change its velocity much.

core.h: Inertial mass and weight are different
core.p: Mass and weight are often confused. Inertial mass is about resistance to acceleration; weight is a gravitational force.
bullets: **Inertial mass** (kg) is the same everywhere: on Earth, on the Moon and in deep space.
**Weight** (N) = mass x gravitational field strength, so it changes with location.
On the Moon (g about 1.6 N/kg) a 60 kg astronaut weighs about 96 N instead of about 600 N on Earth, but is just as hard to accelerate sideways.
In orbit an astronaut feels weightless, yet a heavy piece of equipment is still hard to start and stop moving.
Experiments show that the mass that resists acceleration and the mass that is pulled by gravity are equal, which is why all objects fall with the same acceleration (without air resistance).

callouts.p: An astronaut in orbit still has their full inertial mass, so a big force is still needed to change their velocity quickly.

core.p: Newton's first law is sometimes called the law of inertia. The two ideas describe the same behaviour.
bullets: First law: zero resultant force means no change in velocity.
Inertia: objects tend not to change their velocity.
Inertial mass: tells you **how much** they resist that change.
Second law: how big the change is: a = F / m.
Together: a large resultant force and a small inertial mass give the quickest change of velocity.

callouts.p: First law (no resultant, no change), inertia (tendency not to change), inertial mass (how strongly it resists), second law (how much change for a given force).

core.p: Inertial mass matters just as much for stopping as for starting.
bullets: For a given braking force, the deceleration is a = F / m, so a larger mass decelerates less.
A smaller deceleration means the vehicle takes **more time and more distance** to stop.
This is why lorries keep longer gaps and have lower speed limits on some roads.
Doubling the load roughly halves the deceleration for the same braking force.
Engineers fit larger brakes to heavier vehicles to give a larger braking force.

callouts.p: Write a = F / m and say that a larger m with the same F gives a smaller a: concise and worth the mark.

core.h: Changing direction needs a force too
core.p: Inertia resists any change in velocity, and velocity includes direction.
bullets: A car turning a corner needs a sideways (centripetal) resultant force from friction between tyres and road.
Passengers feel themselves 'thrown' outwards on a bend: in fact their bodies tend to continue in a straight line while the car turns.
On ice, friction is small, so the car tends to keep moving in a straight line and fails to turn.
A heavier vehicle needs a larger sideways force to turn the same corner at the same speed.
A hammer thrower lets go and the hammer flies off in a straight line at a tangent to the circle.

callouts.p: There is no force pushing passengers outwards on a bend. They are continuing in a straight line because of inertia.

core.p: Calculations use inertial mass = force / acceleration. Make sure the force is the **resultant** force.
bullets: Write: m = F / a.
Find the resultant force first if more than one force acts.
Find acceleration from (v - u) / t if needed.
Give the answer in kg.
Check: a heavy object should come out with a large inertial mass; a tiny acceleration for a big force means large mass.

callouts.p: N divided by m/s squared gives kg. If your answer is in some other unit, you have used the wrong quantities.

analogy.p: Inertia is like a trolley's stubbornness: once parked it does not want to move, and once rolling it does not want to stop or turn. Inertial mass is how stubborn it is: a trolley full of bottled water is far more stubborn than an empty one, and you measure that stubbornness by how hard you must push to get a certain speed-up. The analogy breaks down because stubbornness suggests the trolley chooses to resist, and suggests a resisting force; really inertia is a property of matter, not a force, and in space a trolley with no friction would keep rolling forever.

terms.d: The tendency of an object to stay at rest or keep moving at constant velocity unless a resultant force acts on it.
A measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object; inertial mass = force / acceleration.
The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms; the same everywhere.
The gravitational force on an object, W = m g, measured in newtons.
The single force that has the same effect as all the forces on an object combined.
The rate of change of velocity, in m/s squared.
Speed in a stated direction.
With zero resultant force an object stays at rest or keeps moving at constant velocity.
Resultant force = mass x acceleration.
One quantity divided by another; inertial mass is the ratio of force to acceleration.
When one quantity doubles, the other halves; acceleration is inversely proportional to mass for a fixed force.
The force per unit mass due to gravity, about 10 N/kg on Earth and about 1.6 N/kg on the Moon.
A restraint that applies a backward force to decelerate a passenger with the car.
A decrease in velocity, caused by a resultant force opposite to the motion.

mistakes.w: Inertia is the force that keeps an object moving.
mistakes.r: Inertia is a property (tendency to keep its velocity), not a force; no force is needed to keep moving at constant velocity.

mistakes.w: When a car brakes, the passenger is thrown forward by a force.
mistakes.r: The passenger continues moving forward because of inertia while the car decelerates; the seat belt applies a backward force.

mistakes.w: Inertial mass = mass x acceleration.
mistakes.r: Inertial mass = force / acceleration.

mistakes.w: Astronauts in orbit have no mass because they are weightless.
mistakes.r: They still have the same inertial mass; only the apparent weight changes.

mistakes.w: Objects on the Moon are easier to accelerate sideways because they weigh less.
mistakes.r: Inertial mass is the same on the Moon, so the same force gives the same acceleration (ignoring friction).

mistakes.w: A heavier object has less inertia because gravity pulls it more.
mistakes.r: More mass means more inertia: it is harder to change its velocity.

mistakes.w: Inertial mass is measured in newtons.
mistakes.r: Inertial mass is measured in kilograms.

mistakes.w: On a bend, a force pushes passengers outwards.
mistakes.r: Their bodies tend to keep moving in a straight line because of inertia while the car turns.

exam.q: What is meant by inertia?
model: The tendency of an object to remain at rest or to continue moving at constant velocity (unless a resultant force acts)
exam.tip: Include both the 'at rest' and 'moving' cases.

exam.q: Define inertial mass.
model: A measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object
defined as force / acceleration
exam.tip: Two parts: what it measures, and the ratio.

exam.q: A resultant force of 18 N gives an object an acceleration of 1.5 m/s squared. Calculate the inertial mass.
model: = 12 kg
exam.tip: Unit kg.

exam.q: Object A accelerates at 4 m/s squared and object B at 1 m/s squared when the same resultant force acts on each. Which has the larger inertial mass and by what factor?
model: B has the larger inertial mass
4 times larger (since m = F / a and a is 4 times smaller)
exam.tip: Same F, so mass is inversely proportional to a.

exam.q: Explain why a passenger without a seat belt can hit the windscreen when a car stops suddenly.
model: The braking force acts on the car, which decelerates
The passenger has inertia and continues moving forward at the original speed
No (or too small a) backward force acts on the passenger until they hit the windscreen
exam.tip: Avoid saying the passenger is thrown forward by a force.

exam.q: An astronaut on the Moon finds it easier to lift a rock than on Earth, but just as hard to push it to start it rolling along a smooth surface. Explain.
model: Lifting depends on weight; weight = m g
g on the Moon is smaller so the rock's weight is smaller
Starting it moving depends on inertial mass
Inertial mass is the same on the Moon, so the same force is needed for the same acceleration
exam.tip: Separate weight (gravity) from inertial mass (resistance to acceleration).

exam.q: A student plots a graph of resultant force (y-axis) against acceleration (x-axis) for a trolley. The line passes through the origin with a gradient of 0.8. What does the gradient represent and what is its value with unit?
model: The inertial mass of the trolley
0.8 kg
exam.tip: Gradient = rise / run = F / a.

exam.q: Describe how you could measure the inertial mass of a trolley in the laboratory.
model: Pull the trolley with a string over a pulley to hanging masses; force = weight of hanging masses (m g)
Use a card and two light gates (or a data logger) to measure speeds at two points
Calculate acceleration = change in speed / time
Repeat for a range of forces, repeating each and taking means
Compensate for friction (slightly tilt the runway) and keep the total mass being accelerated constant
Plot force against acceleration; the gradient of the line through the origin is the inertial mass
exam.tip: Link the method to the definition m = F / a.

exam.q: Explain why a fully loaded lorry needs a longer distance to stop than the same lorry when empty, for the same braking force.
model: The loaded lorry has a greater inertial mass
For the same force the deceleration is smaller (a = F / m)
So it takes longer and travels further before stopping
exam.tip: Use the equation in words.

exam.q: Explain the coin and card trick: a card is flicked quickly from under a coin resting on top of a glass, and the coin falls into the glass.
model: The coin is at rest and has inertia, so it tends to stay at rest
The friction force from the card acts for a very short time, so it hardly changes the coin's velocity
Once the card is gone, the only force is the coin's weight, so it falls into the glass
exam.tip: Mention why the small brief force produces little change in velocity.

worked.q: A sledge is pulled with a force of 60 N. Friction on it is 15 N. It accelerates at 1.5 m/s squared. Calculate the inertial mass of the sledge and rider.
steps: Resultant force = 60 - 15 = 45 N
Inertial mass = force / acceleration
m = 30 kg
worked.ans: 30 kg

worked.q: A 0.5 kg ball and a 4.0 kg medicine ball are each pushed with a resultant force of 8 N. Calculate each acceleration and compare.
steps: Ball: a = F / m = 8 / 0.5 = 16 m/s squared
Medicine ball: a = 8 / 4.0 = 2 m/s squared
The medicine ball has 8 times the inertial mass
So its acceleration is 8 times smaller: its velocity is harder to change
worked.ans: 16 m/s squared and 2 m/s squared; the medicine ball has 8 times the inertial mass.

worked.q: An astronaut of mass 70 kg is in deep space, far from any planet. A crewmate pushes her with a resultant force of 35 N. Calculate her acceleration and explain why her weightlessness does not make it larger.
steps: Inertial mass is 70 kg everywhere, including in deep space
a = 0.5 m/s squared
Weightlessness means no noticeable gravitational force, but inertial mass, which resists acceleration, is unchanged
worked.ans: 0.5 m/s squared, the same as it would be on a frictionless surface on Earth.

phy_ocra.4.5.summary: **Momentum** is a property of every moving object, defined as **momentum = mass x velocity (p = m v)**, measured in **kg m/s**. Because velocity is a vector, momentum is a vector too, so its direction matters. In a **closed system** (no external forces) the **total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after it**: this is **conservation of momentum**. It lets you predict the velocities of objects after collisions and explosions, such as cars crashing, snooker balls, and a gun recoiling.

core.p: Momentum describes how much 'motion' an object has. It depends on both how much mass is moving and how fast and in which direction it moves.
bullets: **Momentum = mass x velocity**, p = m v.
A heavy lorry and a light car at the same speed: the lorry has more momentum.
A bullet has a small mass but a very large velocity, so it can have a large momentum.
An object at rest has **zero momentum**.
The larger the momentum, the larger the force or the longer the time needed to stop the object.

callouts.p: Momentum is the product of an object's mass and its velocity: momentum (kg m/s) = mass (kg) x velocity (m/s).
p = m v. You need to recall this; it is not on the equation sheet.

core.p: Using SI units makes momentum come out in kg m/s.
bullets: Mass m in **kilograms (kg)**.
Velocity v in **metres per second (m/s)**.
Momentum p in **kilogram metres per second (kg m/s)**.
To find velocity: **v = p / m**. To find mass: **m = p / v**.
Convert grams to kg and km/h to m/s first (divide km/h by 3.6).

callouts.p: Momentum is not measured in newtons or in m/s. Write kg m/s.

core.p: Velocity has a direction, so momentum does too. Two objects can have the same size of momentum but in opposite directions.
bullets: Choose one direction as **positive** (usually to the right).
Velocities, and so momenta, in the opposite direction are **negative**.
A 2 kg ball at 3 m/s to the right has p = +6 kg m/s; at 3 m/s to the left, p = -6 kg m/s.
Two equal and opposite momenta add up to **zero total momentum**.
Getting the signs right is the key to collision and explosion questions.

callouts.p: Write 'taking right as positive' at the start of your working. It shows the examiner you are handling direction.

core.p: When objects interact, they push on each other with equal and opposite forces for the same time, so the momentum one gains is exactly the momentum the other loses.
bullets: In a **closed system**, the **total momentum before = total momentum after** a collision or explosion.
A closed system is one where **no external forces** act (or they are balanced), so nothing from outside adds or removes momentum.
Momentum can be transferred from one object to another, but the total stays the same.
This applies to collisions where objects bounce off, collisions where they stick together, and explosions.
Real situations are only approximately closed: friction and air resistance are external forces that slowly reduce the total.

callouts.p: In a closed system, the total momentum before an event is equal to the total momentum after the event.
Newton's third law: during the collision the forces on the two objects are equal and opposite and act for the same time, so the changes in momentum are equal and opposite.

core.p: If two objects join after a collision, they move off with one shared velocity. Use the combined mass after the collision.
bullets: Total momentum before = m1 u1 + m2 u2.
Total momentum after = (m1 + m2) v.
Set them equal and solve for the unknown.
Example: a 2 kg trolley at 3 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg trolley and they stick: 2 x 3 + 1 x 0 = 3 x v, so v = 2 m/s.
The joined objects always move **more slowly** than the moving object did before, because the same momentum is shared by more mass.

callouts.p: After sticking, add the masses before multiplying by the shared velocity.

fig.cap: A 2 kg trolley at 3 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg trolley and they stick together. Total momentum before = 2 x 3 = 6 kg m/s; after = (2 + 1) x 2 = 6 kg m/s, so momentum is conserved.

core.p: If the objects separate after the collision, each has its own velocity afterwards.
bullets: Total momentum before = m1 u1 + m2 u2.
Total momentum after = m1 v1 + m2 v2.
You will be given all but one value; solve for the unknown.
A velocity that comes out negative means that object moves in the **negative direction** (it has bounced back).
Snooker: a moving cue ball hits a stationary ball head-on; the cue ball nearly stops and the target ball moves off with almost the same velocity, because the balls have equal mass.

callouts.t: Momentum conserved, kinetic energy usually not
callouts.p: Total momentum is conserved in every collision in a closed system, but some kinetic energy is usually transferred to heating and sound, so the kinetic energy after is often less.

core.p: In an explosion the objects start at rest, so the **total momentum before is zero**. It must still be zero afterwards.
bullets: After an explosion the pieces move in **opposite directions** with equal-sized but opposite momenta.
m1 v1 + m2 v2 = 0, so m1 v1 = -m2 v2.
The **lighter** piece moves off **faster**; the heavier piece moves more slowly.
**Gun recoil**: the bullet gains forward momentum, so the gun gains equal backward momentum and recoils.
Other examples: a cannon recoiling, a person jumping off a boat (the boat moves back), two skaters pushing apart, a spring pushing two trolleys apart.
Rockets: exhaust gases are pushed backwards with momentum, so the rocket gains equal forward momentum.

callouts.p: Starting from rest, total momentum = 0 before and after. The momenta of the pieces must cancel out.

fig.cap: Two trolleys at rest are pushed apart by a spring. Total momentum before is zero. After: 2 kg x (-1.5 m/s) + 1 kg x (+3 m/s) = -3 + 3 = 0, so the lighter trolley moves off twice as fast.

core.p: Follow the same steps every time and collision questions become routine.
bullets: 1. Draw a quick before-and-after sketch with masses and velocities.
2. State a positive direction.
3. Work out the total momentum before (add each m v with signs).
4. Write an expression for the total momentum after, including the unknown.
5. Set before = after and solve.
6. Give the answer with unit and direction, and check it is sensible.

callouts.p: Write 'momentum before = momentum after' as a line of working. It often earns the first mark even if later arithmetic goes wrong.

core.p: A momentum bar chart shows how the total is shared out before and after a collision while the total itself stays fixed.
bullets: Before the sticking collision only trolley A is moving: all 6 kg m/s belongs to A.
After the collision A has 2 x 2 = 4 kg m/s and B has 1 x 2 = 2 kg m/s.
The bars are different heights for each object, but the **totals are equal**.
Momentum lost by one object = momentum gained by the other.
The same picture with a zero total describes an explosion.

callouts.p: Momentum is transferred between objects in a collision; it is never created or destroyed in a closed system.

fig.cap: Momentum before and after the sticking collision. Before, trolley A has all 6 kg m/s. After, A has 4 kg m/s and B has 2 kg m/s: the total is still 6 kg m/s.

core.p: Conservation of momentum can be tested with trolleys on a runway, using light gates to measure velocities.
bullets: Fix a card to each trolley and place a light gate before and after the collision point.
Measure the velocity of trolley A before the collision (card length / time).
Use Velcro or a pin and cork so the trolleys stick, or springs so they bounce apart.
Measure the velocity (or velocities) after the collision.
Measure the masses with a balance; calculate total momentum before and after.
Tilt the runway slightly to compensate for friction so the system is closer to closed; the totals should be equal within experimental error.

callouts.t: Why the totals may differ slightly
callouts.p: Friction and air resistance are external forces, and timing and mass measurements have uncertainty. Expect totals to be close, not identical.

core.p: Stopping a moving object means reducing its momentum to zero. How quickly that happens decides how large the force is (the detailed rate-of-change link is a separate point).
bullets: A larger momentum needs a larger force or a longer time to bring it to rest.
Crumple zones, seat belts, airbags, crash helmets, and cushioned playground surfaces all **increase the time** over which momentum changes, which **reduces the force**.
Heavier and faster vehicles have more momentum, so crashes involving them are more dangerous.
Catching a ball: moving your hands back with the ball increases the stopping time and reduces the sting.
In a collision between a car and a lorry, both experience the same size force, but the car (smaller mass) has a much bigger change in velocity.

callouts.p: Safety features do not absorb momentum; they increase the time taken for the momentum to change, so the force is smaller.

analogy.p: Think of momentum as money in a closed room of people. When two people collide, one hands some money to the other: one loses exactly what the other gains, so the total in the room never changes. Money in one pocket going 'left' counts as negative, so two people with equal and opposite amounts have a total of zero, like an explosion from rest. The analogy breaks down because momentum depends on both mass and velocity and is a vector with direction, whereas money is a single positive amount; and real rooms are not perfectly closed, just as friction lets momentum leak out to the Earth.

terms.d: The product of mass and velocity, p = m v, measured in kg m/s.
Speed in a given direction; a vector quantity.
A quantity with both size and direction, such as momentum, velocity and force.
A quantity with size only, such as mass and speed.
In a closed system the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after it.
A system on which no external resultant force acts, so total momentum stays constant.
A force on the system from something outside it, such as friction from the ground.
An event in which two or more objects exert forces on each other for a short time.
An event in which objects initially at rest (or together) are pushed apart.
The backward movement of an object, such as a gun, when it pushes another object forwards.
The total mass of objects that move together after sticking.
Choosing one direction as positive and the opposite as negative.
The unit of momentum: kilogram metres per second.
A sensor that times how long a card blocks a light beam so speed can be calculated.
Part of a car designed to deform in a crash, increasing the collision time and reducing the force.

mistakes.w: Momentum = mass x speed, and direction does not matter.
mistakes.r: Momentum = mass x velocity; it is a vector so direction must be included with a sign.

mistakes.w: Momentum is measured in N or kg/m/s.
mistakes.r: Momentum is measured in kg m/s.

mistakes.w: After an explosion from rest, total momentum is the sum of the sizes of the two momenta.
mistakes.r: The momenta are in opposite directions; the total is zero.

mistakes.w: When two trolleys stick, using only one trolley's mass after the collision.
mistakes.r: Use the combined mass (m1 + m2) after the collision.

mistakes.w: Momentum is conserved in all situations.
mistakes.r: Momentum is conserved in a closed system, where no external forces act.

mistakes.w: Kinetic energy and momentum are both always conserved in collisions.
mistakes.r: Momentum is conserved in a closed system; kinetic energy is often partly transferred to heating and sound.

mistakes.w: The gun recoils because the bullet pushes air back onto it.
mistakes.r: The bullet gains forward momentum so the gun gains equal backward momentum (total stays zero).

mistakes.w: Airbags absorb the momentum of the passenger.
mistakes.r: Airbags increase the time taken for the passenger's momentum to reach zero, reducing the force.

exam.q: Write down the equation linking momentum, mass and velocity.
model: momentum = mass x velocity (p = m v)
exam.tip: Velocity, not speed.

exam.q: Calculate the momentum of a 1500 kg car travelling at 20 m/s.
exam.tip: Include the unit kg m/s.

exam.q: A ball of mass 0.16 kg has a momentum of 4.8 kg m/s. Calculate its velocity.
exam.tip: Rearrange first.

exam.q: State the principle of conservation of momentum.
model: In a closed system (no external forces)
total momentum before an event = total momentum after
exam.tip: The 'closed system' condition is often the second mark.

exam.q: A 3 kg trolley moving at 4 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg trolley. They stick together. Calculate their velocity after the collision.
model: Momentum before = 3 x 4 + 1 x 0 = 12 kg m/s
Momentum after = (3 + 1) x v
exam.tip: Use the combined mass after.

exam.q: A rifle of mass 4.0 kg fires a bullet of mass 0.010 kg at 400 m/s. Calculate the recoil velocity of the rifle.
model: Total momentum before = 0
Momentum of bullet = 0.010 x 400 = 4.0 kg m/s
Rifle velocity = -4.0 / 4.0 = 1.0 m/s backwards (opposite to bullet)
exam.tip: Give the direction of the recoil.

exam.q: Explain why a gun recoils when it is fired.
model: Before firing, total momentum is zero
The bullet gains momentum forwards
Momentum is conserved so the gun must gain equal momentum backwards
exam.tip: Use 'momentum is conserved'.

exam.q: A 0.5 kg ball moving at 6 m/s to the right hits a 1.5 kg ball at rest. After the collision the 0.5 kg ball moves at 3 m/s to the left. Calculate the velocity of the 1.5 kg ball.
model: Taking right as positive, momentum before = 0.5 x 6 = 3 kg m/s
Momentum after = 0.5 x (-3) + 1.5 v
v = 3 m/s to the right
exam.tip: The bounce-back velocity is negative.

exam.q: Describe how you could use trolleys and light gates to show that momentum is conserved in a collision.
model: Measure masses of both trolleys with a balance
Attach cards; measure the velocity of trolley A before collision with a light gate (card length / time)
Trolley B at rest; trolleys collide and stick (Velcro or pin and cork)
Measure the velocity after the collision with a second light gate
Calculate total momentum before (mA uA) and after ((mA + mB) v)
Compensate for friction by tilting the runway; repeat; show totals are equal within experimental error
exam.tip: Say what is measured, how, and how momentum is calculated.

exam.q: Two ice skaters stand at rest together and push apart. Skater A (50 kg) moves off at 2.4 m/s. Skater B moves off at 1.5 m/s in the opposite direction. Calculate the mass of skater B.
model: Total momentum before = 0, so momenta after are equal and opposite
exam.tip: Sizes of the two momenta are equal.

exam.q: Explain why momentum is not quite conserved when two trolleys collide on a rough bench.
model: Friction is an external force acting on the trolleys
so the system is not closed and some momentum is lost (transferred to the Earth)
exam.tip: Name the external force.

worked.q: A 1200 kg car moving at 15 m/s crashes into the back of a stationary 800 kg car. They lock together. Calculate the speed of the wreckage just after the collision.
steps: Momentum before = 1200 x 15 + 800 x 0 = 18 000 kg m/s
Combined mass = 1200 + 800 = 2000 kg
Momentum after = 2000 x v
worked.ans: 9 m/s in the original direction of the moving car

worked.q: A 60 kg person steps forward off a 120 kg boat at rest, moving at 2.0 m/s. Ignoring water resistance, calculate the velocity of the boat.
steps: Total momentum before = 0
Momentum of person = 60 x 2.0 = 120 kg m/s forwards
Boat must have 120 kg m/s backwards
v = 120 / 120 = 1.0 m/s backwards
worked.ans: 1.0 m/s in the opposite direction to the person

worked.q: Two trolleys head towards each other. Trolley A (2.0 kg) moves right at 3.0 m/s; trolley B (1.0 kg) moves left at 2.0 m/s. They stick together. Find the velocity afterwards.
steps: Take right as positive
Momentum before = 2.0 x 3.0 + 1.0 x (-2.0) = 6.0 - 2.0 = 4.0 kg m/s
Combined mass = 3.0 kg
v = 4.0 / 3.0 = 1.3 m/s (to 2 s.f.), positive so to the right
worked.ans: 1.3 m/s to the right

phy_ocra.4.10.summary: An object moving in a circle at constant speed is **constantly accelerating**, because velocity is a vector and its **direction keeps changing** even though its size (the speed) stays the same. By Newton's first and second laws, a changing velocity needs a **resultant force**, and for circular motion this force always acts **towards the centre of the circle**. OCR asks for this qualitatively: explain why constant speed does not mean constant velocity, and name the force that provides the centripetal pull in real examples such as orbits, cars on bends and objects whirled on strings.

core.p: Speed is a **scalar**: it has size (magnitude) only. Velocity is a **vector**: it has size and **direction**. Two objects can have the same speed but different velocities if they move in different directions. This difference is the key to understanding circular motion.
bullets: Speed = distance travelled / time taken (scalar).
Velocity = displacement / time, in a stated direction (vector).
A change in **either** the size **or** the direction of velocity is a change in velocity.
Going round a bend at a steady 20 m/s still changes velocity, because direction changes.

callouts.p: Velocity is the speed of an object in a given direction; it is a vector quantity.

core.h: Why constant speed in a circle means acceleration
core.p: Acceleration is the **rate of change of velocity**. In a circle the direction of motion changes all the time, so the velocity changes all the time, so the object is **accelerating** even though the speedometer reading never changes. This is the big idea OCR tests.
bullets: Acceleration = change in velocity / time taken.
Changing direction alone = changing velocity = acceleration.
At every instant the velocity points along a **tangent** to the circle.
The acceleration points **towards the centre** of the circle.
Because the force is at **90 degrees** to the motion, it changes direction but not speed.

callouts.p: Motion in a circle at constant speed involves a changing velocity, so the object is accelerating and there must be a resultant force.

core.h: Newton's laws applied to circular motion
core.p: Newton's first law says an object keeps moving at **constant velocity** (same speed in a straight line) unless a **resultant force** acts on it. An object in circular motion is not moving in a straight line, so a resultant force must be acting. Newton's second law (F = ma) tells us the force is in the same direction as the acceleration: towards the centre.
bullets: No resultant force: object moves in a **straight line** at constant speed.
Resultant force towards centre: object is pulled round into a circle.
F = m x a, so a bigger mass needs a bigger force for the same circle and speed.
The forces on a circling object are **not balanced**; it is not in equilibrium.

callouts.p: Do not say the forces are balanced because the speed is constant. Balanced forces give constant velocity, i.e. a straight line.

core.p: The resultant force that keeps an object moving in a circle is called the **centripetal force** (centripetal means centre-seeking). It is **not a new kind of force**; it is simply the name for whatever real force, or combination of forces, points to the centre.
bullets: Always directed **towards the centre** of the circle.
Acts at right angles to the velocity.
Provided by tension, gravity, friction, electrostatic attraction or a contact force.
Never draw an extra arrow labelled centripetal force on top of the real forces.

callouts.p: The resultant force acting towards the centre of a circle that keeps an object moving in circular motion.

core.p: At any moment the object is moving along the **tangent** to the circle: a straight line that just touches the circle at that point, at 90 degrees to the radius. If the centripetal force suddenly disappeared, the object would carry on in a straight line along that tangent (Newton's first law).
bullets: Tangent is perpendicular to the radius at that point.
Velocity arrow is drawn along the tangent, in the direction of travel.
Force/acceleration arrow is drawn along the radius, pointing inwards.
If a string snaps, the ball flies off **along the tangent**, not outwards along the radius.

callouts.p: Draw velocity arrows touching the circle and force arrows pointing to the centre. Examiners check both directions.

core.h: What happens if the force is removed
core.p: Removing the centripetal force removes the resultant force, so the object stops accelerating and continues at **constant velocity**: the same speed in a straight line along the tangent at the point of release. This is why a hammer thrower releases at just the right moment.
bullets: String breaks: ball moves off at a tangent.
Car hits ice (little friction): car slides straight on instead of turning.
Gravity switched off (thought experiment): Moon would move off in a straight line.
The object does **not** fly directly away from the centre.

callouts.p: There is no outward centrifugal force pushing objects away. Feeling thrown outwards is your body trying to keep moving in a straight line.

core.h: Factors affecting the size of the force needed
core.p: OCR only requires qualitative ideas, but grade 9 answers can explain trends. A larger centripetal force is needed when the object has **more mass**, is moving **faster**, or moves in a **tighter (smaller radius) circle**, because in each case the velocity must change more sharply or more mass must be accelerated.
bullets: Greater mass: more force for the same acceleration (F = ma).
Greater speed: direction must change faster, so more force.
Smaller radius: tighter turn, so more force.
If the force available is too small, the object moves into a wider path or slides off.

callouts.p: On wet or icy roads the maximum friction is lower, so cars must slow down on bends or they cannot get enough centripetal force.

core.h: Orbits of planets, moons and satellites
core.p: A planet, moon or satellite in a circular orbit moves at constant speed but is constantly accelerating towards the body it orbits. **Gravity** provides the centripetal force. The object is continually falling towards the centre but moving sideways fast enough to keep missing it.
bullets: Gravity acts along the line joining the two centres, so it points to the centre of the orbit.
Speed is constant in a circular orbit, so kinetic energy is constant.
Gravity is perpendicular to the motion, so it does **no work** on the object in a circular orbit.
Satellites closer to Earth must travel faster to stay in orbit.

callouts.p: For orbit questions always name gravity (gravitational attraction) as the force and say it acts towards the centre.

core.p: Everyday examples let you apply the idea. On a level road, **friction** between tyres and road acts sideways towards the centre of the bend. On a fairground ride or in a spin dryer, the wall pushes inwards on the person or clothes.
bullets: Car on a bend: sideways friction from road on tyres, towards centre.
Passenger in car: seat belt, seat or door pushes them inwards.
Spin dryer: drum wall pushes clothes inwards; water escapes through holes along tangents.
Cyclist leaning into a bend: friction at the tyres provides the inward force.

core.h: Energy and work in uniform circular motion
core.p: Work done = force x distance moved **in the direction of the force**. The centripetal force is always at 90 degrees to the motion, so it does **no work**. This explains why the speed, and therefore the kinetic energy, stays constant.
bullets: Force perpendicular to motion: no energy transferred by that force.
Kinetic energy store stays the same in uniform circular motion.
Only a force component along the direction of motion can change speed.

callouts.p: Force perpendicular to velocity changes direction only; force along velocity changes speed only.

core.p: Six-mark questions reward a clear chain of reasoning. Link each step with because or so: direction changing, so velocity changing, so accelerating, so resultant force, which acts towards the centre, provided by a named force.
bullets: Step 1: velocity is a vector (speed and direction).
Step 2: direction changes continuously, so velocity changes.
Step 3: changing velocity means acceleration.
Step 4: acceleration requires a resultant force (Newton's first and second laws).
Step 5: force acts towards the centre (centripetal).
Step 6: name what provides it in this situation.

callouts.p: Use the words vector, direction, accelerating, resultant force and towards the centre: these are the mark-scheme keywords.

analogy.t: A dog on a lead running round you
analogy.p: Imagine a dog that always wants to run straight ahead, held on a tight lead while you stand still. The dog keeps running at the same speed, but the lead keeps tugging it inwards towards you, so its path bends into a circle. The lead is the centripetal force (tension) and the dog's wish to go straight is inertia. Let go and the dog runs off in a straight line, not directly away from you. Where it breaks down: a real dog chooses its own direction using its legs and friction, whereas a ball on a string has no intention; also a dog is not moving at perfectly constant speed.

terms.d: A quantity with magnitude (size) only, e.g. speed, distance, mass.
A quantity with magnitude and direction, e.g. velocity, force, acceleration.
Distance travelled per unit time; a scalar.
Speed in a given direction; a vector.
The rate of change of velocity; a vector.
The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object combined.
Motion in a circle at constant speed.
The resultant force towards the centre of the circle that keeps an object moving in a circle.
The acceleration of an object in circular motion, directed towards the centre.
A straight line that touches a circle at one point, at right angles to the radius; the direction of velocity.
The distance from the centre of a circle to its edge.
The tendency of an object to stay at rest or keep moving at constant velocity.
The curved path of a planet, moon or satellite around a larger body, maintained by gravity.
The pulling force in a stretched string, rope or cable.
A force that opposes the relative motion of surfaces in contact.

mistakes.w: The object is not accelerating because its speed is constant.
mistakes.r: It is accelerating because its direction, and so its velocity, is changing.

mistakes.w: Velocity is constant in a circle.
mistakes.r: Speed is constant; velocity changes because direction changes.

mistakes.w: The forces on it are balanced.
mistakes.r: There is a resultant (unbalanced) force towards the centre.

mistakes.w: Centrifugal force pushes it outwards.
mistakes.r: The resultant force acts inwards, towards the centre; there is no outward force on the object.

mistakes.w: When the string breaks the ball flies straight outwards.
mistakes.r: It moves off in a straight line along the tangent to the circle.

mistakes.w: The centripetal force acts in the direction of motion.
mistakes.r: It acts at right angles to the motion, towards the centre.

mistakes.w: Centripetal force is an extra force added to the free body diagram.
mistakes.r: It is provided by a real force such as tension, gravity or friction.

mistakes.w: The Moon stays up because there is no gravity in space.
mistakes.r: Gravity provides the centripetal force that keeps the Moon in orbit.

exam.q: State the difference between speed and velocity.
model: Velocity has direction (is a vector) but speed does not (is a scalar).
exam.tip: Use the words scalar and vector.

exam.q: A satellite moves in a circular orbit at constant speed. Explain why it is accelerating.
model: Its direction of motion is constantly changing, so its velocity is changing.
Acceleration is a change in velocity, so it is accelerating.
exam.tip: Link direction to velocity to acceleration.

exam.q: State the direction of the resultant force on an object moving in a circle at constant speed.
model: Towards the centre of the circle.
exam.tip: Do not say inwards without saying towards the centre.

exam.q: Name the force that provides the centripetal force for the Moon orbiting the Earth.
model: Gravity / gravitational attraction of the Earth.
exam.tip: Weight is accepted by some schemes but gravitational force is safest.

exam.q: A car travels round a roundabout at a steady 10 m/s. Name the force that keeps it moving in a circle and give its direction.
model: Friction (between tyres and road).
Acting towards the centre of the roundabout.
exam.tip: Two marks: name and direction.

exam.q: A ball on a string is whirled in a horizontal circle. The string breaks. Describe the motion of the ball immediately afterwards and explain your answer.
model: Ball moves in a straight line along the tangent to the circle (in the direction it was moving).
Because there is no longer a resultant force, so velocity stays constant (Newton's first law).
exam.tip: Say tangent, not outwards.

exam.q: Explain why the centripetal force does not change the speed of an object in uniform circular motion.
model: The force acts at right angles to the direction of motion.
So no work is done / no energy is transferred to the kinetic store, only direction changes.
exam.tip: Use the 90 degree idea.

exam.q: A student says: the forces on a fairground chair moving round in a circle at constant speed must be balanced. Evaluate this statement.
model: The statement is wrong.
Velocity is changing (direction), so there must be a resultant force towards the centre.
exam.tip: State clearly whether you agree, then justify.

exam.q: A car is driven round the same bend faster. Explain why it is more likely to skid.
model: A larger centripetal force is needed at higher speed.
Friction may not be large enough to provide it, so the car cannot follow the curve.
exam.tip: Mention that friction has a maximum value.

exam.q: Explain, using Newton's laws, why a satellite moving at constant speed in a circular orbit must have a force acting on it and describe this force.
model: Velocity is a vector, with magnitude and direction.
In a circular orbit the direction of motion changes continuously.
So velocity changes, which means the satellite is accelerating.
Newton's first law: without a resultant force it would move in a straight line at constant speed.
Newton's second law: acceleration requires a resultant force in the same direction as the acceleration.
The force is towards the centre of the orbit (centripetal) and is provided by Earth's gravitational attraction; it is perpendicular to the motion so speed stays constant.
exam.tip: Six-mark answers need a logical chain using the key words.

worked.q: A toy train goes round a circular track at a steady 0.5 m/s. Is its velocity constant? Is it accelerating? Explain.
steps: Speed is 0.5 m/s all the time, so speed is constant.
The train's direction keeps changing as it goes round the track.
Velocity includes direction, so velocity is changing.
A changing velocity is an acceleration, directed towards the centre.
A resultant force must act towards the centre: the contact force from the rails on the wheels.
worked.ans: Velocity is not constant; the train is accelerating towards the centre even though its speed is constant.

worked.q: An athlete swings a hammer in a circle and releases it. Draw arrows (in words) for the velocity and the force on the hammer just before release, and describe the path just after release.
steps: Just before release, velocity is along the tangent to the circle in the direction of motion.
The force on the hammer (tension in the wire) points along the wire towards the athlete, the centre of the circle.
On release the tension becomes zero, so there is no horizontal resultant force.
Horizontally the hammer carries on at the velocity it had at the moment of release, along the tangent.
Gravity then pulls it downwards, so it follows a curved path towards the ground.
worked.ans: Velocity along the tangent, force towards the centre; after release the hammer moves off along the tangent (and falls under gravity).

worked.q: Two identical cars go round the same bend, car A at 15 m/s and car B at 25 m/s. Which needs the larger resultant force and what provides it?
steps: Both cars have the same mass and follow the same radius.
Car B is faster, so its direction must change more quickly.
So car B has a larger centripetal acceleration.
F = ma with the same m, so car B needs a larger force.
The force is provided by friction between the tyres and the road, towards the centre of the bend.
worked.ans: Car B needs the larger centripetal force, provided by friction from the road towards the centre of the bend.

phy_ocra.4.6.summary: Force, mass, velocity and acceleration are tied together by Newton's second law: a resultant force F acting on a mass m produces an acceleration a, so F = m x a, and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, a = (v - u) / t. Combining these gives the triple-only idea that **force equals rate of change of momentum**, F = (mv - mu) / t. This explains why safety features such as crumple zones, airbags, seat belts and helmets work: they make the change in momentum happen over a **longer time**, so the force on the person is **smaller**.

core.h: The key quantities and their units
core.p: Before linking anything, you must know exactly what each quantity is, whether it is a vector or scalar, and its SI unit. Force, velocity, acceleration and momentum are all **vectors**, so their direction matters and a negative sign simply means the opposite direction.
bullets: **Force (F)**: a push or pull, measured in **newtons (N)**, vector.
**Mass (m)**: the amount of matter in an object, measured in **kilograms (kg)**, scalar.
**Velocity (v)**: speed in a stated direction, measured in **metres per second (m/s)**, vector.
**Acceleration (a)**: rate of change of velocity, measured in **m/s²**, vector.
**Momentum (p)**: mass x velocity, measured in **kg m/s**, vector.
**Time (t)**: measured in **seconds (s)**; always convert minutes or milliseconds first.
1 N is the resultant force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s², so 1 N = 1 kg m/s².

callouts.p: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: acceleration = change in velocity / time taken.

core.p: Acceleration tells you how quickly velocity changes. If velocity changes by a lot in a short time, the acceleration is large. Because velocity is a vector, slowing down is a **negative acceleration** (deceleration).
bullets: Equation: **acceleration = change in velocity / time**, a = (v - u) / t.
u is the initial velocity, v is the final velocity.
If v is less than u, a is negative: the object is **decelerating**.
Rearranged: v = u + at and t = (v - u) / a.
On a velocity-time graph, acceleration is the **gradient** of the line.
A steeper gradient means a larger acceleration; a horizontal line means zero acceleration (constant velocity).

callouts.p: If a question asks for deceleration, give the size as a positive number, e.g. a deceleration of 4 m/s² is the same as an acceleration of -4 m/s².

fig.cap: Velocity-time graph for uniform acceleration. The gradient (change in velocity divided by change in time) equals the acceleration.

core.p: Newton's second law says that the acceleration of an object is **directly proportional to the resultant force** on it and **inversely proportional to its mass**. Doubling the resultant force doubles the acceleration; doubling the mass halves it.
bullets: Equation: **resultant force (N) = mass (kg) x acceleration (m/s²)**, F = ma.
It must be the **resultant** (net) force, not just one of the forces.
The acceleration is always in the **same direction as the resultant force**.
a = F / m: a bigger mass needs a bigger force for the same acceleration.
m = F / a: this ratio is the inertial mass.
If the resultant force is zero, a = 0, so velocity stays constant (links to the first law).

callouts.p: F = ma uses the RESULTANT force. Always find the resultant force first by adding forces in the same direction and subtracting opposing ones.

core.p: Most mistakes in F = ma questions come from using the wrong force. Draw a quick free body diagram, decide on a positive direction, and combine the forces along that line before you use the equation.
bullets: Forces in the same direction **add**.
Forces in opposite directions **subtract**.
Driving force minus resistive forces (friction, air resistance, drag) = resultant force.
For a falling object: resultant = weight - air resistance.
For a rocket taking off: resultant = thrust - weight.
If the resultant comes out negative, the object accelerates in the negative direction (or decelerates).

callouts.p: Using the driving force in F = ma when friction is also acting. The question will often give you both forces deliberately.

core.p: Momentum is a measure of how hard it is to stop a moving object. It depends on both mass and velocity, so a slow lorry and a fast bullet can both have large momentum.
bullets: Equation: **momentum (kg m/s) = mass (kg) x velocity (m/s)**, p = mv.
Momentum is a **vector**: it has the same direction as the velocity.
Change in momentum = final momentum - initial momentum = mv - mu.
If an object reverses direction, the change in momentum is larger than either momentum alone because the signs differ.
A stationary object has zero momentum.

callouts.p: Momentum = mass x velocity. It is a vector quantity measured in kg m/s.

core.h: Force as rate of change of momentum (triple, higher)
core.p: Substituting a = (v - u) / t into F = ma gives F = m(v - u) / t = (mv - mu) / t. This is Newton's second law in its most general form: **the resultant force on an object equals its rate of change of momentum**.
bullets: Equation: **force (N) = change in momentum (kg m/s) / time (s)**, F = Δp / t.
Change in momentum = force x time (F x t), sometimes called impulse.
For a given change in momentum, a **longer time gives a smaller force**.
For a given change in momentum, a **shorter time gives a larger force**.
The force on an object is equal and opposite to the force it exerts on what it hits (third law link).
Derivation: F = ma and a = (v - u)/t so F = m(v - u)/t = (mv - mu)/t.

callouts.p: Force = change in momentum / time. Increasing the collision time reduces the rate of change of momentum, which reduces the force.

core.h: Using F = (mv - mu) / t in calculations
core.p: Treat momentum questions methodically: pick a positive direction, work out initial and final momentum with signs, find the change, then divide by the time.
bullets: Step 1: choose a positive direction.
Step 2: initial momentum = m x u; final momentum = m x v (include signs).
Step 3: change in momentum = mv - mu.
Step 4: force = change in momentum / time.
Convert time to seconds: 50 ms = 0.050 s.
A negative answer means the force acts opposite to your chosen positive direction.
If an object bounces back, v and u have opposite signs, so the change is the sum of their sizes.

callouts.p: A 0.5 kg ball hitting a wall at 10 m/s and rebounding at 8 m/s has a change in momentum of 0.5 x (8 - (-10)) = 9 kg m/s, not 1 kg m/s.

core.p: In a crash the car and passengers must lose all their momentum. The change in momentum is fixed by the mass and speed, so the only way to reduce the force on the passengers is to make the stopping **take longer**.
bullets: **Crumple zones**: the front and back of the car deform on impact, increasing the time taken for the car to stop.
**Seat belts**: stretch slightly, increasing the time for the passenger to stop and spreading the force over the chest.
**Airbags**: inflate and slowly deflate as the head hits them, increasing the stopping time and spreading the force over a bigger area.
**Collapsible steering columns** and **padded dashboards** also increase stopping time.
Each feature: same change in momentum, **longer time**, so **smaller rate of change of momentum**, so **smaller force**, so less injury.
Seat belts must be replaced after a crash because they have been permanently stretched.

callouts.p: For 4 to 6 marks write the full chain: increases time to stop, same change in momentum, so rate of change of momentum is smaller, so force is smaller, so fewer injuries.

core.p: The same idea explains lots of everyday design and sporting technique. Anything that lengthens the time of an impact reduces the force; anything that shortens it increases the force.
bullets: **Cycle and motorcycle helmets**: crushable foam lengthens impact time.
**Crash mats and soft playground surfaces**: deform to increase the time a falling child takes to stop.
**Bending your knees** when you land after a jump increases stopping time and reduces force on the legs.
**Catching a ball**: moving your hands back with the ball increases the time, so it stings less.
**Following through** in golf, tennis or cricket keeps the club or bat in contact longer, giving a bigger change in momentum so the ball leaves faster.
**Packaging** such as bubble wrap and polystyrene increases the stopping time of fragile items.
**Hammers**: a hard head stops in a very short time, giving a very large force on the nail.

core.p: OCR expects you to estimate the forces and decelerations involved in road transport. Large decelerations cause serious injury because the forces on the body are large.
bullets: Typical car mass: about 1000 to 1500 kg; typical person: about 70 kg.
A car at about 13 m/s (30 mph) stopping in a crash in about 0.1 s has a deceleration of about 130 m/s².
Force on a 70 kg passenger: F = ma = 70 x 130, about 9000 N.
If a safety feature makes that stop take 0.5 s instead, the force falls to about 1800 N.
Use a = (v - u)/t then F = ma, or F = (mv - mu)/t directly; both give the same answer.
Doubling the stopping time halves the force.

callouts.p: In an estimate question, state your assumed values clearly and round sensibly. Examiners give marks for reasonable assumptions and correct method.

core.p: Many 1 and 2 mark questions test the relationships rather than the numbers. Use the equations to reason about what changes when one quantity is altered.
bullets: F = ma: at constant mass, **a is directly proportional to F**.
F = ma: at constant force, **a is inversely proportional to m**.
F = Δp / t: at constant Δp, **F is inversely proportional to t**.
p = mv: at constant mass, momentum is directly proportional to velocity.
Doubling speed doubles momentum, so doubles the force needed to stop in the same time.

core.p: These equations are on the recall list, so you need to know them without the equation sheet and be able to rearrange them.
bullets: **force = mass x acceleration** (F = ma).
**momentum = mass x velocity** (p = mv).
**acceleration = change in velocity / time** (a = Δv / t).
Triple, higher: **force = change in momentum / time** (F = (mv - mu) / t).
Always write the equation, substitute with units, then give the answer with a unit.

callouts.p: Even if your final answer is wrong, writing the equation and a correct substitution usually earns method marks.

analogy.p: Imagine a loaded shopping trolley rolling towards you. Its momentum is how much stopping it needs. You could stop it with a sudden hard shove (short time, big force, sore hands) or by walking backwards with it and slowing it gently (long time, small force). Either way you remove the same amount of momentum. Crumple zones and airbags are the walking-backwards method. The analogy breaks down because a real crash happens in a fraction of a second, the forces vary during the impact, and the car also transfers energy into deforming metal rather than just being slowed by a steady push.

terms.d: The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object combined.
The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms; a scalar.
Speed in a given direction; a vector measured in m/s.
The rate of change of velocity, measured in m/s².
A negative acceleration: the velocity decreasing with time.
The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the resultant force and inversely proportional to its mass, F = ma.
Mass multiplied by velocity, a vector measured in kg m/s.
Final momentum minus initial momentum, mv - mu.
Change in momentum divided by the time taken; equal to the resultant force.
Force multiplied by the time it acts for; equal to the change in momentum.
The force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s².
A measure of how difficult it is to change an object's velocity; the ratio of force to acceleration.
A part of a car designed to deform in a collision, increasing the time to stop and reducing the force.
A bag that inflates in a crash so the occupant stops over a longer time and larger area, reducing force.
A quantity with both magnitude and direction.
Equal to the acceleration of the object.

mistakes.w: Crumple zones reduce the change in momentum.
mistakes.r: The change in momentum is the same; crumple zones increase the time taken, so the rate of change of momentum and the force are smaller.

mistakes.w: Airbags absorb the force.
mistakes.r: Airbags increase the time taken for the head to stop (and spread the force over a larger area), so the force is reduced.

mistakes.w: Using the driving force in F = ma when friction acts.
mistakes.r: Use the resultant force: driving force minus resistive forces.

mistakes.w: Momentum is measured in N or kg/m/s.
mistakes.r: Momentum is measured in kg m/s.

mistakes.w: A ball that rebounds has a change in momentum of m(v - u) using sizes only.
mistakes.r: Take direction into account: the velocities have opposite signs, so the change is m(v + u) in size.

mistakes.w: Using time in milliseconds directly in F = Δp/t.
mistakes.r: Convert to seconds first, e.g. 20 ms = 0.020 s.

mistakes.w: A bigger mass means a bigger acceleration.
mistakes.r: For the same resultant force, a bigger mass gives a smaller acceleration (a = F/m).

mistakes.w: Seat belts work by stopping you moving.
mistakes.r: Seat belts stretch, increasing the time for you to stop, so the force on you is smaller.

mistakes.w: Acceleration = velocity / time.
mistakes.r: Acceleration = change in velocity / time taken.

exam.q: State the equation linking resultant force, mass and acceleration.
model: resultant force = mass x acceleration (F = ma)
exam.tip: Words or standard symbols are both accepted.

exam.q: A car of mass 1200 kg accelerates at 2.5 m/s². Calculate the resultant force on the car.
exam.tip: Always give the unit.

exam.q: A 0.40 kg ball accelerates from rest to 15 m/s. Calculate the change in momentum of the ball.
model: change in momentum = m(v - u) = 0.40 x (15 - 0)
= 6.0 kg m/s
exam.tip: From rest means u = 0.

exam.q: A cyclist and bike of total mass 80 kg have a forward force of 200 N and resistive forces of 120 N. Calculate the acceleration.
model: resultant force = 200 - 120 = 80 N
exam.tip: Find the resultant force before using F = ma.

exam.q: A tennis ball of mass 0.058 kg changes velocity from 0 to 40 m/s while in contact with a racket for 0.005 s. Calculate the average force on the ball.
model: change in momentum = 0.058 x 40 = 2.32 kg m/s
F = change in momentum / time = 2.32 / 0.005
exam.tip: This is the triple-only equation F = (mv - mu)/t.

exam.q: Explain why a person who bends their knees on landing is less likely to be injured.
model: bending knees increases the time taken to stop
change in momentum is the same
so rate of change of momentum / force is smaller
exam.tip: Name all three links: time, same momentum change, smaller force.

exam.q: Explain how a crumple zone reduces injuries to passengers in a crash.
model: crumple zone deforms / crumples on impact
this increases the time taken for the car (and passengers) to stop
the change in momentum is the same
so the rate of change of momentum is smaller, so the force on passengers is smaller
exam.tip: Avoid saying it absorbs the force or reduces momentum.

exam.q: A 70 kg passenger travelling at 15 m/s is brought to rest by a seat belt in 0.30 s. Without a seat belt they would stop in 0.020 s against the dashboard. Calculate both forces and comment on the difference.
model: change in momentum = 70 x 15 = 1050 kg m/s
with seat belt F = 1050 / 0.30 = 3500 N
without seat belt F = 1050 / 0.020 = 52 500 N
force without seat belt is 15 times larger, so much more likely to cause injury
exam.tip: Compare with a ratio to earn the evaluation mark.

exam.q: Describe the relationship between resultant force, mass and acceleration.
model: acceleration is directly proportional to resultant force (for constant mass)
acceleration is inversely proportional to mass (for constant force)
exam.tip: State which quantity is held constant.

exam.q: Use the equations F = ma and a = (v - u)/t to show that force equals rate of change of momentum.
model: substitute a: F = m(v - u)/t
= (mv - mu)/t which is change in momentum / time
exam.tip: Show each algebraic step clearly.

exam.q: Car manufacturers fit crumple zones, airbags and seat belts. Explain, using ideas about momentum and forces, how these features protect passengers. Include an estimate of the forces involved.
model: in a crash the car and passengers lose all their momentum
the change in momentum is fixed by mass and velocity
crumple zones deform, increasing the time for the car to stop
seat belts stretch and airbags deflate, increasing the time for passengers to stop
longer time gives smaller rate of change of momentum, so smaller force (F = Δp/t)
airbags and seat belts spread the force over a larger area, reducing pressure
estimate: 70 kg person at 13 m/s stopping in 0.1 s feels about 9000 N; stopping in 0.5 s reduces this to about 1800 N
exam.tip: Level 3 answers link every feature to time and force and include a sensible numerical estimate.

worked.q: A lorry of mass 12 000 kg slows from 20 m/s to 8 m/s in 6.0 s. Calculate its deceleration and the resultant braking force.
steps: a = -2.0 m/s², so the deceleration is 2.0 m/s²
F = 24 000 N acting backwards
worked.ans: Deceleration 2.0 m/s²; resultant braking force 24 000 N (2.4 x 10^4 N).

worked.q: A 0.15 kg cricket ball travelling at 30 m/s towards a bat is hit straight back at 25 m/s. The contact time is 1.5 ms. Calculate the average force on the ball.
steps: Take the direction the ball leaves the bat as positive: u = -30 m/s, v = +25 m/s.
initial momentum = 0.15 x (-30) = -4.5 kg m/s
final momentum = 0.15 x 25 = 3.75 kg m/s
change in momentum = 3.75 - (-4.5) = 8.25 kg m/s
worked.ans: Average force = 5500 N in the direction the ball leaves the bat.

worked.q: A 60 kg stunt performer falls and hits the ground at 8.0 m/s. Compare the force on landing on concrete (stops in 0.010 s) and on a crash mat (stops in 0.40 s).
steps: change in momentum = 60 x 8.0 = 480 kg m/s
crash mat: F = 480 / 0.40 = 1200 N
worked.ans: The crash mat reduces the force from 48 000 N to 1200 N, 40 times smaller, because it increases the stopping time 40 times.

phy_ocra.4.7.summary: When a force moves an object through a distance along the line of action of the force, **work is done** and energy is transferred from one store to another. The amount of work done is calculated using **work done = force x distance (along the line of action of the force)**, measured in joules, where **1 joule = 1 newton-metre**. Work done against friction or air resistance transfers energy to the **thermal store** of the objects and surroundings, which is why brakes and sliding surfaces get hot.

core.p: In physics, work is not just effort. **Work is done whenever a force moves an object through a distance in the direction of the force.** Doing work is one of the ways energy is transferred between stores, so work done always equals energy transferred.
bullets: Work is done only if there is **movement along the line of action of the force**.
Pushing a wall that does not move: no distance, so **no work is done** on the wall.
Carrying a bag horizontally at constant height: the lifting force is upwards but the movement is sideways, so the lifting force does no work on the bag.
**Work done = energy transferred**: if 500 J of work is done, 500 J of energy has moved between stores.
Work is a scalar; it is measured in **joules (J)**.
Transferring energy by a force is called transfer **mechanically** (by forces doing work).

callouts.p: Work is done when a force moves an object through a distance. Work done = force x distance moved along the line of action of the force.

core.p: This is a recall equation: you must know it and rearrange it. The distance must be the distance moved **in the direction of the force** (along its line of action).
bullets: **work done (J) = force (N) x distance (m)** (along the line of action of the force).
Symbols: W = F x d (some books write E = F x d).
Rearranged: F = W / d and d = W / F.
Doubling the force at the same distance doubles the work done.
Doubling the distance at the same force doubles the work done.
Convert distances to metres (e.g. 50 cm = 0.50 m) and forces to newtons (e.g. 2 kN = 2000 N).

callouts.p: work done = force x distance (along the line of action of the force). This is on the recall list.

core.p: Because work done = force x distance, the unit of work can be written as newton x metre. OCR expects you to be able to convert between the two.
bullets: **1 joule = 1 newton-metre** (1 J = 1 N m).
One joule of work is done when a force of 1 N moves an object 1 m along its line of action.
Do not confuse this with the moment of a force, which is also written in N m but is a turning effect, not energy.

callouts.p: One joule is the work done when a force of one newton moves an object one metre in the direction of the force.

core.p: To describe what happens when work is done, say which **store** energy leaves, which store it goes to, and the **pathway** it uses. Doing work by a force is the mechanical pathway.
bullets: Stores: **kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, chemical, magnetic, electrostatic, nuclear**.
Pathways: **mechanically** (forces doing work), **electrically** (current doing work), **by heating**, **by radiation** (light, sound waves).
Example: kicking a ball transfers energy mechanically from the chemical store of the player to the kinetic store of the ball.
Example: lifting a book transfers energy from the chemical store of your muscles to the gravitational potential store of the book.
Example: stretching a spring transfers energy to its elastic potential store.
Energy is always **conserved**: the total in a closed system stays the same; it is just moved between stores.

head: Situation
Energy from
Energy to
rows: Kinetic store of car (and thermal store)
Thermal store of brakes and surroundings
Pushing a box at constant speed
Thermal store of box, floor and surroundings

core.p: When you lift an object at a steady speed, the upward force equals its weight. The work done against gravity is stored in the object's **gravitational potential energy store**.
bullets: Work done lifting = weight x vertical height = F x h.
Weight = mass x gravitational field strength (W = mg), so work done = mgh.
Only the **vertical height** counts for work done against gravity, not the length of a ramp or stairs.
The work done lifting equals the **gain in gravitational potential energy**.
Lowering an object: gravity does work on it and energy leaves the GPE store.

callouts.p: Pushing a box up a ramp: the force along the ramp x the ramp length gives the work you do. Some goes into GPE (weight x vertical height) and the rest is wasted against friction.

fig.cap: Lifting a box with a 30 N force (equal to its weight) through a vertical height of 2.0 m does 60 J of work, which is transferred to the box's gravitational potential energy store.

core.h: Work done against friction causes heating
core.p: When surfaces rub together, the force of friction opposes the motion. Work done against friction transfers energy to the **thermal store** of the surfaces and the surroundings, so they get warmer. This energy is usually wasted (dissipated).
bullets: Rubbing your hands together: work done against friction warms your hands.
Pushing a box across a floor at constant speed: all the work you do goes into the thermal store of box, floor and air.
Air resistance and drag are frictional forces; work done against them heats the air and the object.
A meteor heats up and glows because of work done against air resistance.
Reducing friction (lubrication with oil, streamlining) reduces wasted energy.
Energy dissipated to the surroundings spreads out and is hard to use again.

callouts.p: Say energy is transferred to the thermal store, not that friction 'creates heat' or 'uses up energy'. Energy is never created or destroyed.

core.h: Braking: work done to stop a vehicle
core.p: When a driver brakes, the friction force between the brake pads and the discs does work on the wheels. This transfers energy from the **kinetic store** of the vehicle to the **thermal store** of the brakes, which can get very hot.
bullets: Work done by brakes = braking force x braking distance.
To stop completely, work done by brakes = kinetic energy of the vehicle: F x d = ½ m v².
For the same braking force, **doubling the speed gives four times the kinetic energy**, so four times the braking distance.
Larger braking forces give large decelerations, which can make brakes overheat or tyres skid.
A heavier vehicle at the same speed has more kinetic energy, so it needs more work done to stop it.

callouts.p: Brakes apply friction, friction does work, energy moves from the kinetic store of the car to the thermal store of the brakes, the car slows down and the brakes get hot.
