core.p: OCR questions often ask you to describe all the changes in the way energy is stored when a system changes. Identify the system, the stores at the start and end, and the work done by each force.
bullets: Ball thrown upwards: kinetic store decreases, gravitational store increases; some energy goes to thermal store of air (air resistance).
Object accelerated by a constant force: work done by resultant force increases the kinetic store.
Vehicle slowing down: kinetic store decreases; thermal store of brakes increases.
Bringing water to boil in a kettle: electrical work increases thermal store of water (not mechanical, but same idea of work transferring energy).
Moving vehicle hitting an obstacle: kinetic store transferred to thermal stores and work done deforming the vehicle.
Always state where energy starts, where it ends, and the mechanism (which force does the work).

callouts.p: For full marks name both stores AND the pathway: 'energy is transferred mechanically by the frictional force from the kinetic store of the car to the thermal store of the brakes'.

core.p: Students lose marks by assuming any force does work. A force only does work on an object if the object moves along the line of action of that force.
bullets: Holding a heavy weight still: no movement, so no work done on the weight (your muscles get tired because of internal processes, not work on the weight).
A satellite in circular orbit: gravity acts towards the centre, at right angles to the motion, so gravity does no work and the speed stays constant.
Reaction force from the floor on a sliding box: acts upwards, motion is sideways, so it does no work.
A force at an angle: only the part of the movement in the direction of the force counts.

callouts.p: Holding a box still feels hard, but in physics no work is done on the box because it does not move.

core.p: In real machines not all the work done ends up in the useful store. The rest is dissipated, usually by work done against friction, heating the surroundings.
bullets: Useful work done + wasted energy = total work done (input energy).
Efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input (as a decimal or x100 for %).
Lubrication reduces friction so less work is wasted.
Streamlining reduces air resistance on vehicles, so less fuel is needed.
No machine can be more than 100% efficient because energy cannot be created.

core.p: Use a consistent method in every work-done question so you collect all the method marks.
bullets: Write the equation: work done = force x distance.
Check the distance is along the line of action of the force (vertical height for lifting).
Convert units: kN to N, cm or km to m, kJ to J.
Substitute with units and calculate.
State the answer with the unit J (or N m if asked).
Where needed, link to another equation: e.g. W = mgh for lifting, or W = ½ m v² for stopping a moving object.

callouts.p: If a question gives mass instead of force when lifting, find the weight first with W = mg (g = 10 N/kg on OCR papers), then use work done = weight x height.

analogy.t: Work done as paying for a journey
analogy.p: Think of energy as money in bank accounts (stores). Doing work is like paying for a journey: the force is the price per metre and the distance is how far you travel, so the total bill is force x distance. The money leaves one account (say your chemical store) and lands in another (kinetic, gravitational or thermal). Friction is like a fee that goes to the surroundings and can never be spent again. The analogy breaks down because money can be printed or destroyed, whereas energy is always conserved, and because work is only paid when movement is in the direction of the force.

terms.d: Energy transferred when a force moves an object a distance along the line of action of the force.
The straight line along which a force acts; only movement along it counts towards work done.
The unit of energy and work; 1 J is the work done when 1 N moves an object 1 m.
Equal to one joule when used for work done or energy.
A way energy is held, e.g. kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, chemical.
Energy an object has because it is moving.
Energy an object has because of its height in a gravitational field.
Energy stored in a stretched, compressed or bent object.
Energy stored in an object due to its temperature.
Energy transfer by a force moving an object (work done by a force).
A force that opposes motion between surfaces in contact; work done against it heats the surfaces.
Energy spreading out into the surroundings, usually as thermal energy, so it is less useful.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores.
An object or group of objects being studied.
Useful energy output divided by total energy input.

mistakes.w: Work done = force / distance or force x time.
mistakes.r: Work done = force x distance moved along the line of action of the force.

mistakes.w: Holding a heavy box still does work on the box.
mistakes.r: No work is done on the box because it does not move a distance.

mistakes.w: Friction creates heat energy.
mistakes.r: Work done against friction transfers energy to the thermal store of the surfaces and surroundings.

mistakes.w: Energy is lost when a car brakes.
mistakes.r: Energy is transferred from the kinetic store to the thermal store of the brakes and surroundings; it is dissipated, not destroyed.

mistakes.w: Using the length of a ramp for work done against gravity.
mistakes.r: Use the vertical height for work done against gravity (gain in GPE).

mistakes.w: Using mass in kg as the force.
mistakes.r: Convert mass to weight first using W = mg before using work done = force x distance.
1 J = 1 N m (newton-metre).

mistakes.w: Doubling speed doubles the braking distance.
mistakes.r: Kinetic energy depends on v², so doubling speed gives four times the work needed and four times the braking distance for the same force.

mistakes.w: Saying energy is transferred 'by friction' with no stores named.
mistakes.r: Name the stores: from the kinetic store of the object to the thermal store of the surfaces and surroundings.

exam.q: State the equation linking work done, force and distance.
model: work done = force x distance (along the line of action of the force)
exam.tip: Include 'along the line of action' if asked to define.

exam.q: Convert 450 N m into joules.
exam.tip: 1 N m = 1 J.

exam.q: A person pushes a trolley with a force of 60 N for 25 m. Calculate the work done.
model: W = F x d = 60 x 25
exam.tip: Always include the unit.

exam.q: A crane does 36 000 J of work lifting a load 12 m. Calculate the force applied by the crane.
exam.tip: Rearrange before substituting.

exam.q: A student holds a 20 N bag still for 2 minutes. Explain why no work is done on the bag.
model: work is only done when a force moves an object a distance
the bag does not move so distance = 0 and work done = 0
exam.tip: Link to the equation W = F x d.

exam.q: Describe the energy transfer when a box is pushed across a rough floor at constant speed.
model: work is done against friction
energy transferred from chemical store of person
to thermal store of box, floor and surroundings (kinetic store unchanged as speed is constant)
exam.tip: Constant speed means no gain in kinetic energy.

exam.q: A 2.5 kg book is lifted onto a shelf 1.6 m high. Calculate the work done. (g = 10 N/kg)
model: weight = mg = 2.5 x 10 = 25 N
W = F x d = 25 x 1.6
exam.tip: Convert mass to weight first.

exam.q: A car of mass 1000 kg travelling at 20 m/s brakes to a stop. The braking force is 5000 N. Calculate the braking distance.
model: kinetic energy = ½ m v² = 0.5 x 1000 x 20² = 200 000 J
work done by brakes = kinetic energy lost
exam.tip: Equate work done by the brakes to the kinetic energy lost.

exam.q: Explain why the brakes of a car get hot when the car stops.
model: friction between brake pads and discs does work
energy is transferred from the kinetic store of the car
to the thermal store of the brakes, increasing their temperature
exam.tip: Name the force, the starting store and the end store.

exam.q: Explain why the braking distance of a car is four times larger when its speed doubles, if the braking force is the same.
model: kinetic energy = ½ m v², so doubling v gives four times the kinetic energy
work done by brakes must equal kinetic energy, and work done = F x d
with the same F, d must be four times larger
exam.tip: Use both equations in the explanation.

exam.q: A cyclist freewheels down a hill, then brakes to stop at the bottom. Describe all the changes in the way energy is stored during this journey and explain the role of work done by forces.
model: at the top, energy is in the gravitational potential store of cyclist and bike
going down, gravity does work, so the GPE store decreases and the kinetic store increases
air resistance and friction do work against the motion, transferring some energy to the thermal store of the surroundings
when braking, friction in the brakes does work on the wheels
energy moves from the kinetic store to the thermal store of the brakes, which warm up
total energy is conserved; the energy ends up dissipated in the surroundings
exam.tip: A logical sequence naming stores, forces and conservation reaches Level 3.

worked.q: A tractor pulls a plough with a force of 4.5 kN over a distance of 0.80 km. Calculate the work done in MJ.
steps: Convert: F = 4.5 kN = 4500 N; d = 0.80 km = 800 m
worked.ans: Work done = 3.6 MJ (3.6 x 10^6 J).

worked.q: A 60 kg student climbs stairs with a vertical height of 4.0 m. The staircase is 7.0 m long. Calculate the work done against gravity. (g = 10 N/kg)
steps: Weight = mg = 60 x 10 = 600 N
Use the vertical height, not the stair length: d = 4.0 m
This 2400 J goes into the student's gravitational potential energy store.
worked.ans: Work done against gravity = 2400 J.

worked.q: A sledge is pulled 30 m at constant speed across snow with a horizontal force of 40 N. Calculate the work done and describe where the energy goes.
steps: Constant speed means the kinetic store does not change.
The pulling force balances friction, so all the work done is against friction.
The 1200 J is transferred to the thermal store of the sledge, snow and surroundings.
worked.ans: 1200 J of work is done, all transferred to thermal stores (dissipated) because the speed is constant.

phy_ocra.4.8.summary: Power is the **rate at which energy is transferred**, or the rate at which work is done. It is calculated using **power = work done / time** (or energy transferred / time) and measured in **watts**, where **1 watt = 1 joule per second**. Two machines can do exactly the same work, but the one that does it in less time has the greater power, which is why power ratings are used to compare motors, engines, appliances and even people climbing stairs.

core.p: Power tells you **how quickly** energy is transferred, not how much. A powerful motor and a weak motor can both lift the same load to the same height (same work done), but the powerful one does it faster.
bullets: **Power is the rate of energy transfer** (or the rate of doing work).
Power is a **scalar** quantity.
More energy transferred in the same time means more power.
The same energy transferred in less time means more power.
Power ratings on appliances show how many joules they transfer each second.

callouts.p: Power is the rate at which energy is transferred or the rate at which work is done.

core.p: This is a recall equation. You need to know it, rearrange it and use the correct units.
bullets: **power (W) = work done (J) / time (s)**.
Equivalently: **power (W) = energy transferred (J) / time (s)**, P = E / t.
Rearranged: E = P x t and t = E / P.
Time must be in **seconds**: 2 minutes = 120 s, 1 hour = 3600 s.
Energy must be in **joules**: 1 kJ = 1000 J.

callouts.p: power = work done / time. Work done = energy transferred, so power = energy transferred / time.

core.p: Because power is joules divided by seconds, its unit is joules per second, given the special name the watt.
bullets: **1 watt = 1 joule per second** (1 W = 1 J/s).
1 kilowatt (kW) = 1000 W.
1 megawatt (MW) = 1 000 000 W.
A 60 W lamp transfers 60 J of energy every second.
A 2 kW kettle transfers 2000 J every second.

callouts.p: One watt is a rate of energy transfer of one joule per second.

core.h: Comparing power: same work, different time
core.p: The clearest way to understand power is to compare two objects doing the same job. Work done depends only on force and distance, so time is what makes the difference.
bullets: Two students of equal weight climbing the same stairs do the **same work** against gravity.
The student who climbs faster has a **greater power**.
Halving the time doubles the power for the same work.
A car with a more powerful engine can accelerate to the same speed in a shorter time, because it transfers energy to the kinetic store faster.
A more powerful crane can lift the same load the same height in less time.

core.p: If you plot energy transferred (or work done) against time, the **gradient** of the line is the power. A steeper line means energy is transferred faster.
bullets: Gradient = change in energy / change in time = power.
A straight line means constant power.
A steeper line means a greater power.
A curve that gets less steep shows the power decreasing.
Reading two points from the line and dividing gives the power.

core.h: Measuring the power of a motor
core.p: A simple experiment measures the output power of an electric motor by timing how long it takes to lift a known weight through a measured height.
bullets: Hang a known mass from a string wound onto the motor spindle.
Measure the weight: W = mg (g = 10 N/kg).
Measure the height lifted with a metre rule.
Time the lift with a stopwatch.
Work done = weight x height; power = work done / time.
Repeat and take a mean to reduce the effect of random errors (e.g. reaction time).
The motor's output power is less than its electrical input power because some energy is dissipated by friction and heating.

callouts.p: Lift through a larger height so the time is longer; reaction time then causes a smaller percentage error. Light gates or data loggers can replace the stopwatch.

core.p: A common practical is to measure the power a person develops when running up stairs or doing step-ups.
bullets: Measure the person's mass on scales and calculate weight W = mg.
Measure the vertical height of the stairs (height of one step x number of steps).
Time the climb with a stopwatch.
Work done = weight x vertical height.
Power = work done / time.
Typical values: a student running upstairs develops a few hundred watts.

callouts.p: Use the vertical height of the stairs, not the length along the staircase, because work against gravity depends only on vertical height.

core.p: Real devices waste some of the energy they transfer, usually by heating the surroundings. Efficiency can be calculated from energies or from powers.
bullets: Efficiency = useful power output / total power input.
Efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input.
Multiply by 100 to give a percentage.
Wasted power = total power input - useful power output.
An efficiency can never be greater than 1 (100%).
Example: a 500 W motor with 400 W useful output is 400 / 500 = 0.80 (80%) efficient.

callouts.p: When using efficiency with powers, make sure both powers are in the same unit (both W or both kW).

core.p: The power rating on an appliance tells you how much energy it transfers per second when working normally. A higher power rating means more energy transferred in the same time, which usually costs more to run.
bullets: Kettle: about 2 to 3 kW (heats water quickly).
Microwave oven: about 800 W to 1 kW.
LED lamp: around 5 to 10 W.
Car engine: tens of kilowatts.
Energy transferred = power x time, so leaving a high-power device on for longer transfers more energy.
Comparing a 2 kW and a 1 kW heater: in the same time, the 2 kW heater transfers twice as much energy.

core.h: Explaining power in vehicles and lifting
core.p: Exam questions often ask why one car, lift or crane is more powerful than another. Always link power to energy transferred AND time.
bullets: A more powerful car transfers more energy per second to its kinetic store, so it reaches a given speed in less time.
A more powerful lift raises the same passengers through the same height in less time.
To lift a heavier load in the same time, more work is done, so more power is needed.
Power can be limited by friction: more power is needed to maintain speed against large resistive forces.

callouts.p: Power is not force. A more powerful machine is not necessarily one that exerts a larger force; it is one that transfers energy faster.

core.p: Use a clear method to get full marks on power calculations, which are often combined with work done or weight.
bullets: Step 1: find the work done or energy transferred (use W = F x d or W = mg x h if needed).
Step 2: convert time to seconds.
Step 3: write P = E / t, substitute and calculate.
Step 4: give the unit W (or kW if asked).
For energy questions use E = P x t, with P in W and t in s to get J.
Check your answer is sensible: people develop hundreds of watts, cars tens of kilowatts.

callouts.p: A very common slip is to leave power in kW and time in minutes. Convert both: 1.5 kW for 2 minutes = 1500 W x 120 s = 180 000 J.

analogy.p: Think of energy as water filling a bath. The total water that ends up in the bath is the energy transferred (work done). Power is how fast the tap runs, in litres per second. A wide-open tap (high power) and a dribbling tap (low power) can fill the same bath, but the wide-open tap does it much faster. The analogy breaks down because some energy is always wasted by heating the surroundings, which would be like water splashing out of the bath, and because energy is not a physical substance.

terms.d: The rate at which energy is transferred or work is done.
The unit of power; 1 W = 1 joule per second.
1000 watts.
Energy transferred when a force moves an object along its line of action; work done = force x distance.
The amount of energy moved from one store to another, in joules.
The unit of energy and work done.
How quickly something happens, i.e. an amount per unit time.
The power of an appliance when operating normally, showing the energy it transfers each second.
Useful power (or energy) output divided by total power (or energy) input.
The rate at which energy is transferred to the wanted store.
The rate at which energy is dissipated to unwanted stores, usually thermal.
The force on a mass due to gravity, W = mg, measured in newtons.
Equal to the power.

mistakes.w: Power is the amount of energy a device has.
mistakes.r: Power is the rate of energy transfer: energy transferred per second.

mistakes.w: Power = energy x time.
mistakes.r: Power = energy transferred / time; energy = power x time.

mistakes.w: A more powerful machine does more work.
mistakes.r: A more powerful machine does work faster; for the same task it does the same work in less time.

mistakes.w: 1 W = 1 J/min or 1 J x s.
Using time in minutes or hours in P = E / t.
mistakes.r: Convert time to seconds first.

mistakes.w: Using kW with J to get W directly.
mistakes.r: Convert kW to W (x1000) before calculating, or keep units consistent.

mistakes.w: Using mass instead of weight when finding work done climbing stairs.
mistakes.r: Calculate weight = mg first, then work done = weight x vertical height.

mistakes.w: Power and force are the same thing.
mistakes.r: Force is measured in N; power is energy transfer per second in W.

exam.q: Define power.
model: the rate of energy transfer / rate of doing work (energy transferred per second)
exam.tip: Use the word rate.

exam.q: State the unit of power and what it is equal to in joules and seconds.
model: watt (W)
1 W = 1 J/s
exam.tip: Both parts are needed for 2 marks.

exam.q: A lamp transfers 3600 J in 60 s. Calculate its power.
exam.tip: Show the equation and substitution.

exam.q: A 2.0 kW kettle is switched on for 3 minutes. Calculate the energy transferred.
model: P = 2000 W and t = 180 s
exam.tip: Convert both kW and minutes.

exam.q: A motor does 4500 J of work in 15 s. Calculate its power.
exam.tip: Work done can be used in place of energy transferred.

exam.q: Two cranes lift identical loads to the same height. Crane X takes 20 s and crane Y takes 40 s. Compare the work done and the power of the cranes.
model: both cranes do the same work (same force, same distance)
crane X takes half the time
so crane X has twice the power of crane Y
exam.tip: Comment on work done and power separately.

exam.q: A student of mass 50 kg runs up stairs of vertical height 4.0 m in 5.0 s. Calculate the student's power. (g = 10 N/kg)
model: weight = mg = 50 x 10 = 500 N
work done = 500 x 4.0 = 2000 J
exam.tip: Three linked equations: weight, work done, power.

exam.q: An electric motor has an input power of 250 W and a useful output power of 200 W. Calculate its efficiency.
model: efficiency = useful power output / total power input = 200 / 250
exam.tip: Efficiency has no unit.

exam.q: Explain why a car with a more powerful engine can accelerate to 30 m/s more quickly than a car with a less powerful engine of the same mass.
model: both cars need the same kinetic energy to reach 30 m/s (same mass and speed)
the more powerful engine transfers energy at a greater rate / more energy per second
so it transfers the required energy in less time
exam.tip: Link power to energy and time.

exam.q: Describe how you would measure the output power of a small electric motor that lifts a mass. Include the measurements, equipment and calculation.
model: attach a known mass to a string wound on the motor spindle and calculate weight W = mg
measure the height the mass is lifted using a metre rule
measure the time for the lift with a stopwatch
calculate work done = weight x height
calculate power = work done / time
repeat and calculate a mean; lift through a large height to reduce timing errors
control variables such as supply voltage and the mass used
exam.tip: Level 3 answers give a clear method, equations and ways to improve accuracy.

worked.q: A lift raises 8 people of total mass 600 kg through a height of 30 m in 25 s. Calculate the useful power output of the lift motor. (g = 10 N/kg)
steps: weight = mg = 600 x 10 = 6000 N
work done = weight x height = 6000 x 30 = 180 000 J
worked.ans: Useful power output = 7200 W (7.2 kW).

worked.q: A 1.2 kW microwave oven heats food for 2 minutes 30 seconds. Calculate the energy transferred in kJ.
steps: t = 2 minutes 30 s = 150 s
worked.ans: Energy transferred = 180 kJ.

worked.q: An electric motor with an input power of 800 W lifts a 40 kg load 6.0 m in 4.0 s. Calculate the useful output power and the efficiency. (g = 10 N/kg)
steps: weight = 40 x 10 = 400 N
work done = 400 x 6.0 = 2400 J
useful power = 2400 / 4.0 = 600 W
efficiency = 600 / 800 = 0.75
worked.ans: Useful output power = 600 W; efficiency = 0.75 (75%).

phy_ocra.4.9.summary: Newton's third law states that **when two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal in size and opposite in direction**. These two forces form an **interaction pair**: they are always the **same type of force** and act on **different objects**, so they never cancel each other out. The law explains walking, swimming, rockets and recoil, and must be kept separate from the idea of balanced forces on a single object in equilibrium.

core.p: Forces always come in pairs. You cannot push something without it pushing back on you. Newton's third law describes this pairing exactly.
bullets: **When two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on each other.**
If object A exerts a force on object B, then B exerts a force of **equal size** in the **opposite direction** on A.
The two forces exist at the same time: one cannot happen without the other.
This is true whether the objects are moving or stationary, accelerating or not.
It applies to contact forces (pushes, friction) and non-contact forces (gravity, magnetism, electrostatic).

callouts.p: When two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

core.p: A pair of forces only counts as a Newton's third law pair if it passes every one of these tests. This is what examiners check.
bullets: **Equal in size** (magnitude).
**Opposite in direction**.
**Act on different objects** (one on A, one on B).
**Same type of force** (both gravitational, both contact, both magnetic...).
**Act along the same line**.
Exist for the same length of time.

callouts.p: Third law forces act on DIFFERENT objects, so they can never cancel out or produce equilibrium on their own.

core.p: When two skaters on ice push each other, each feels a force of the same size pushing them backwards. Both move apart, even if only one of them actively pushes.
bullets: Skater A pushes B forwards; B pushes A backwards with an equal force.
The forces are equal, but the **accelerations need not be**: a = F / m.
The lighter skater has the larger acceleration and moves away faster.
This links to momentum: the two skaters gain equal and opposite momentum, so total momentum stays zero.

core.p: Students often think that if forces are equal, the effects must be equal. They are not, because each force acts on a different mass.
bullets: An apple falling: the Earth pulls the apple down with a force equal to the apple's weight.
The apple pulls the Earth up with an **equal** gravitational force.
The Earth's mass is enormous, so its acceleration (a = F / m) is far too small to notice.
A car hitting a fly: the force on the fly equals the force on the car, but the fly's tiny mass means a huge acceleration.
Use F = ma for each object separately to compare the effects.

callouts.p: 'The lorry exerts a bigger force on the car in a crash' is wrong. The forces are equal; the car has the larger acceleration because its mass is smaller.

core.p: A rocket works even in space with nothing to push against, because it pushes on its own exhaust gases.
bullets: The rocket engine pushes hot exhaust gases **downwards (backwards)**.
The gases push the rocket **upwards (forwards)** with an equal force, called **thrust**.
The rocket does not need air to push against: the interaction is between rocket and gas.
Jet engines push air backwards; the air pushes the plane forwards.
If thrust is greater than weight plus drag, there is a resultant upward force and the rocket accelerates (second law).

core.p: You move forwards because something else pushes you forwards, and that push is the third law partner of your own push backwards.
bullets: **Walking**: your foot pushes backwards on the ground (friction); the ground pushes forwards on your foot with an equal force.
On ice there is little friction, so you cannot push backwards hard and the ground cannot push you forwards much, so you slip.
**Swimming**: your hands and feet push water backwards; the water pushes you forwards.
**Rowing**: the oar pushes water backwards; the water pushes the oar (and boat) forwards.
**Car tyres**: the tyres push backwards on the road; the road pushes forwards on the tyres (the driving force).

callouts.p: Always write 'X exerts a force on Y' and 'Y exerts an equal and opposite force on X'. Naming the two objects earns the marks.

core.p: When a gun fires a bullet, or a cannon fires a cannonball, the weapon moves backwards. This is recoil, explained by the third law (and by conservation of momentum).
bullets: The gun pushes the bullet forwards with a large force.
The bullet pushes the gun backwards with an equal force.
The gun has a much larger mass, so its backward acceleration and recoil velocity are much smaller.
Total momentum before firing is zero, so after firing the bullet and gun have equal and opposite momenta.
Stepping off a small boat onto a jetty pushes the boat away from the jetty for the same reason.

core.p: OCR expects you to apply Newton's third law to equilibrium situations, and to avoid confusing third law pairs with balanced forces. A book resting on a table is the classic example.
bullets: Forces **on the book**: its weight (Earth pulls book down) and the normal contact force (table pushes book up).
These two are **balanced**: equal, opposite and on the same object, so the book is in **equilibrium** (first law).
They are **not** a third law pair: they are different types of force and act on the same object.
Third law partner of the table pushing up on the book: **the book pushes down on the table**.
Third law partner of the Earth pulling the book down: **the book pulls the Earth up** (gravitationally).
Third law explains why the contact forces are equal: book and table push on each other equally.

callouts.p: The weight of the book and the reaction from the table are NOT a Newton's third law pair. They act on the same object and are different types of force.

core.p: During a collision the two objects push on each other with equal and opposite forces for the same time. This is why momentum is conserved.
bullets: Car A hits car B: the force of A on B equals the force of B on A, but in the opposite direction.
Both forces act for the same contact time.
Change in momentum = force x time, so the changes in momentum are equal and opposite.
Therefore the total momentum of the two cars is unchanged (conserved).
The car with smaller mass has the larger change in velocity, which is why occupants of lighter cars tend to suffer worse injuries.

callouts.p: Newton's third law (equal and opposite forces for equal times) is the reason why momentum is conserved in collisions and explosions.

core.p: Third law pairs are not just pushes. Any interaction between two objects produces a pair, even at a distance.
bullets: **Gravitational**: Earth pulls Moon; Moon pulls Earth with an equal force (causing tides).
**Magnetic**: two magnets attract or repel each other with equal and opposite forces, even if one is much stronger.
**Electrostatic**: two charged balloons repel each other with equal and opposite forces.
Example: a strong magnet and a small paperclip attract each other with equal forces; the paperclip moves because its mass is small.

core.h: How to identify a third law pair in an exam
core.p: Use a simple sentence template to find the partner of any force. This works for every situation.
bullets: Write the force as: '**A** exerts a [type] force on **B** in [direction]'.
Swap the objects and reverse the direction: '**B** exerts a [type] force on **A** in [opposite direction]'.
Keep the type of force the same.
State that the two forces are equal in size.
Check the two forces act on different objects: if they act on the same object, it is not a third law pair.

callouts.p: Force of person on wall (contact, to the right) pairs with force of wall on person (contact, to the left), equal size.

analogy.p: A handshake cannot be one-sided: when you grip someone's hand, their hand presses back on yours at the same moment. Neither of you can push without being pushed. That is Newton's third law: interactions always involve two objects and two equal forces. The analogy breaks down because in a handshake people can squeeze with different strengths, whereas in physics the two forces are always exactly equal, and a handshake suggests both objects choose to act, whereas a book on a table pushes back without 'trying'.

terms.d: When two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on each other.
Two forces that are equal in size, opposite in direction, of the same type and act on two different objects.
A situation in which two objects exert forces on each other.
The force a surface exerts at right angles to itself on an object in contact with it.
The gravitational force of the Earth on an object, W = mg.
Forces on the same object whose resultant is zero.
The state of an object when the resultant force on it is zero, so it stays at rest or moves at constant velocity.
The single force with the same effect as all the forces acting on an object.
The forward force on a rocket or jet produced by pushing gases backwards.
The backward movement of a gun or cannon when it fires, due to the equal and opposite force from the projectile.
A force that acts only when objects touch, e.g. friction, normal contact force.
A force that acts at a distance through a field, e.g. gravitational, magnetic, electrostatic.
A contact force that opposes relative motion between surfaces.
In a closed system the total momentum before an interaction equals the total momentum after it.

mistakes.w: The weight of a book and the normal contact force from the table are a Newton's third law pair.
mistakes.r: They act on the same object and are different types of force, so they are balanced forces, not a third law pair.

mistakes.w: Third law forces cancel out so nothing can move.
mistakes.r: They act on different objects, so they cannot cancel each other.

mistakes.w: In a crash the heavier vehicle exerts a bigger force.
mistakes.r: Both vehicles exert equal and opposite forces on each other; the lighter one has a bigger acceleration.

mistakes.w: Rockets need air to push against.
mistakes.r: A rocket pushes on its exhaust gases and the gases push back on the rocket, so it works in a vacuum.

mistakes.w: Only the object doing the pushing feels a force.
mistakes.r: Both objects experience a force of equal size.

mistakes.w: The Earth does not feel a force from a falling apple.
mistakes.r: The apple pulls the Earth with an equal force, but the Earth's huge mass means its acceleration is negligible.

mistakes.w: Third law pairs are equal and opposite forces (with nothing more).
mistakes.r: Also state they act on different objects and are the same type of force.

mistakes.w: When you walk, you push yourself forwards.
mistakes.r: Your foot pushes the ground backwards; the ground pushes your foot forwards with an equal force.

exam.q: State Newton's third law.
model: when two objects interact they exert equal and opposite forces on each other
exam.tip: Include 'two objects' and 'equal and opposite'.

exam.q: A person pushes on a wall with a force of 80 N. State the size and direction of the force the wall exerts on the person.
model: in the opposite direction (away from the wall / towards the person)
exam.tip: Size and direction are separate marks.

exam.q: Give two ways in which the forces in a Newton's third law pair are different from a pair of balanced forces.
model: third law pair act on different objects (balanced forces act on the same object)
third law pair are always the same type of force (balanced forces can be different types)
exam.tip: Compare both types of pair in each point.

exam.q: A book rests on a table. A student says the weight of the book and the upward force from the table are a Newton's third law pair. Explain why the student is wrong.
model: both forces act on the same object (the book)
they are different types of force (gravitational and contact)
the partner of the book's weight is the book pulling the Earth upwards (or partner of table on book is book on table)
exam.tip: Name the correct partner for the third mark.

exam.q: Explain, using Newton's third law, how a swimmer moves forwards.
model: the swimmer pushes water backwards
the water pushes the swimmer forwards
with an equal (and opposite) force
exam.tip: Name both objects in each force.

exam.q: Explain how a rocket can accelerate in space where there is no air.
model: rocket pushes exhaust gases backwards / out
gases exert an equal and opposite force on the rocket (thrust)
this gives a resultant force on the rocket so it accelerates; it does not need air to push against
exam.tip: Link third law (force) to second law (acceleration).

exam.q: An apple falls towards the Earth. Explain why the Earth does not noticeably move towards the apple.
model: the apple pulls the Earth with an equal and opposite force
acceleration = force / mass
the Earth's mass is huge, so its acceleration is negligible
exam.tip: Use a = F/m to explain different effects.

exam.q: A small car and a lorry collide. Compare the forces on each vehicle and explain why the car's occupants are more likely to be injured.
model: the forces on each vehicle are equal in size
and opposite in direction (third law)
the car has a much smaller mass
so the car has a much larger deceleration / change in velocity, giving larger forces on its occupants
exam.tip: Do not say the lorry exerts a bigger force.

exam.q: A gun of mass 2.0 kg fires a bullet. During firing the force on the bullet is 500 N. State the force on the gun and calculate the initial acceleration of the gun.
model: force on gun = 500 N backwards
exam.tip: Third law gives the force; second law gives the acceleration.

exam.q: A person stands still on the floor. Describe and explain all the forces acting, identifying which forces are Newton's third law pairs and which are balanced forces.
model: the Earth pulls the person down (weight)
the floor pushes up on the person (normal contact force)
these two forces act on the person, are equal and opposite, so the person is in equilibrium (balanced, first law)
they are not a third law pair because they act on the same object and are different types
the person pushes down on the floor; this pairs with the floor pushing up on the person (contact pair)
the person pulls the Earth up gravitationally; this pairs with the Earth pulling the person down (gravitational pair)
exam.tip: Level 3 answers identify both third law pairs and explain why the balanced pair is not a third law pair.

worked.q: An ice skater of mass 60 kg pushes a second skater of mass 40 kg with a force of 120 N. Calculate the acceleration of each skater.
steps: Third law: the second skater pushes the first with 120 N in the opposite direction.
First skater: a = F / m = 120 / 60 = 2.0 m/s² backwards
Second skater: a = F / m = 120 / 40 = 3.0 m/s² forwards
Equal forces, but the lighter skater accelerates more.
worked.ans: 60 kg skater: 2.0 m/s²; 40 kg skater: 3.0 m/s², in opposite directions.

worked.q: A 3.0 kg box rests on a shelf. Identify the Newton's third law partner of each force acting on the box. (g = 10 N/kg)
steps: Weight of box = mg = 3.0 x 10 = 30 N downwards (Earth pulls box). Partner: box pulls Earth up with 30 N (gravitational).
Normal contact force from shelf = 30 N upwards (shelf pushes box). Partner: box pushes shelf down with 30 N (contact).
The weight and the normal contact force are balanced forces on the box, so it is in equilibrium; they are not a third law pair.
worked.ans: Partners: box pulls Earth up with 30 N; box pushes shelf down with 30 N.

worked.q: A rocket of mass 50 000 kg has engines that push exhaust gases with a force of 800 000 N. Calculate the resultant force on the rocket at lift-off and its acceleration. (g = 10 N/kg)
steps: Third law: gases push the rocket up with 800 000 N (thrust).
Weight = mg = 50 000 x 10 = 500 000 N downwards
Resultant force = 800 000 - 500 000 = 300 000 N upwards
worked.ans: Resultant force 300 000 N upwards; acceleration 6.0 m/s² upwards.
